knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vertexwise root-bound criteria for spanning-arborescence packings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives feasibility criteria for upper, lower, and simultaneous vertexwise bounds on the roots of edge-disjoint spanning arborescences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(U,A)$. (A) There exist $k$ edge-disjoint spanning arborescences such that each $v\in U$ is a root at most $g(v)$ times if and only if every subpartition $\{X_1,\ldots,X_t\}$ of $U$ satisfies $\sum_{i=1}^t\varrho_D(X_i)\ge k(t-1)$ and every $\varnothing\subset X\subseteq U$ satisfies $\widetilde g(X)\ge k-\varrho_D(X)$. (B) There exist such arborescences with each $v$ a root at least $f(v)$ times if and only if $\widetilde f(U)\le k$ and every partition $\{X_0,X_1,\ldots,X_t\}$ of $U$, where $t\ge1$ and only $X_0$ may be empty, satisfies $\sum_{i=1}^t\varrho_D(X_i)\ge k(t-1)+\widetilde f(X_0)$. (C) A packing satisfying both lower bounds $f$ and upper bounds $g$ exists if and only if the lower-bound and upper-bound problems are each separately feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper root bounds are feasible exactly under the unrestricted packing inequalities plus the upper-bound cut inequalities; lower root bounds are feasible exactly under the total lower-bound and partition inequalities; both sets of bounds are jointly feasible exactly when their two one-sided problems are separately feasible.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ and }g\text{ are vertexwise lower and upper root-multiplicity bounds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\exists\text{ upper-bounded packing}\iff\bigl[\forall\text{ subpartitions},\ \sum_i\varrho_D(X_i)\ge k(t-1)\bigr]\land\bigl[\forall\varnothing\subset X\subseteq U,\ \widetilde g(X)\ge k-\varrho_D(X)\bigr],\\&\exists\text{ lower-bounded packing}\iff\widetilde f(U)\le k\land\bigl[\forall\text{ admissible partitions},\ \sum_i\varrho_D(X_i)\ge k(t-1)+\widetilde f(X_0)\bigr],\\&\exists\text{ packing satisfying both bounds}\iff\text{the two one-sided problems are separately feasible}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forests, trees, and spanning-tree characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions and structural facts for finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A forest is a graph with no circuits, and a tree is a connected forest. If a forest (V,E) has \kappa components, then |E|=|V|-\kappa; hence a tree has |E|=|V|-1. Every forest having at least one edge has an end vertex, and a connected subgraph of a tree T is a subtree of T. For F\subseteq E(G), F is a forest when (V,F) is a forest and is a spanning tree when (V,F) is a tree. Moreover, G has a spanning tree if and only if G is connected. If G is connected, then F is a spanning tree if and only if F is an inclusionwise maximal forest, if and only if F is an inclusionwise minimal edge set such that (V,F) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forests are acyclic graphs and trees are connected forests. A forest with κ components has |V|−κ edges, while a tree has |V|−1. A graph has a spanning tree exactly when it is connected; in a connected graph, spanning trees are exactly the maximal forests and the minimal connected spanning edge sets.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
\kappa\text{ is the number of components of the relevant forest}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |E|=|V|-\kappa;\quad G\text{ is connected}\Longleftrightarrow G\text{ has a spanning tree};\quad F\text{ is a spanning tree}\Longleftrightarrow F\text{ is an inclusionwise maximal forest}\Longleftrightarrow (V,F)\text{ is inclusionwise minimally connected}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cuts, bridges, forests, trees, and bonds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational undirected spanning and cut structures in a connected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For connected \(G=(V,E)\), a cut \(\Delta(X)\) separates \(s,t\) when \(|X\cap\{s,t\}|=1\); it is a star-cut when one shore is a singleton. A one-edge cut consists of a cut-edge (isthmus), and \(e\) is a cut-edge iff deleting \(e\) increases the number of connected components by exactly one. A forest is an undirected graph all of whose edges are cut-edges; a tree is a connected forest, equivalently a minimally connected graph; a spanning tree of \(G\) is a spanning subgraph that is a tree. A nonempty cut is elementary (a bond) iff it properly contains no nonempty cut.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cut separates two vertices when exactly one lies on either shore. Star-cuts have a singleton shore. Cut-edges are exactly the edges whose deletion raises the component count by one. Forests have only cut-edges; trees are connected forests, equivalently minimally connected graphs; spanning trees are spanning tree subgraphs. Inclusion-minimal nonempty cuts are bonds.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e\text{ is a cut-edge}\iff c(G-e)=c(G)+1;\quad G\text{ is a tree}\iff G\text{ is minimally connected}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cross-edge relative to a rooted spanning tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a non-tree edge whose endpoints lie in distinct branches relative to the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $F$ be a spanning tree of an undirected graph and let $s$ be a distinguished vertex. A non-tree edge $uv$ is a cross-edge with respect to $s$ if the vertex of the unique $F$-path between $u$ and $v$ that is closest to $s$ is distinct from both $u$ and $v$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative to a rooted spanning tree, a non-tree edge is a cross-edge when the closest-to-root vertex on the tree path between its endpoints is neither endpoint.
assumptions_latex: $F$ is a spanning tree of an undirected graph
$P_F(u,v)$ is the unique tree path joining $u$ and $v$
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: uv\text{ is a cross-edge with respect to }s\iff \arg\min_{x\in V(P_F(u,v))}d_F(s,x)\notin\{u,v\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary structural properties of finite trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects leaf existence, the connected edge-count characterization, unique paths, and the unique-cycle effect of adding an edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite simple undirected graphs: (a) every tree with more than one node has at least one leaf; (b) an undirected graph \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\) is a tree if and only if it is connected and \(|\mathcal E|=|\mathcal N|-1\); (c) every two distinct nodes of a tree are joined by a unique path; and (d) if \(e\) is a new edge joining two distinct nodes of a tree \(T\), then \(T+e\) contains exactly one cycle, counted as an unoriented cyclic subgraph rather than by alternative traversal descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite tree with more than one node has a leaf. A finite undirected graph is a tree exactly when it is connected and has one fewer edge than nodes. Every two distinct tree nodes have a unique path between them, and adding a new edge between two tree nodes creates one cycle, without counting alternate descriptions of that same cycle separately.
assumptions_latex: G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\text{ is a finite simple undirected graph}
T\text{ is a tree in the clauses concerning trees}
e=\{u,v\}\notin E(T),\quad u,v\in V(T),\quad u\ne v\text{ in clause (d)}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |V(T)|>1\Rightarrow T\text{ has a leaf};\quad G\text{ is a tree}\iff G\text{ is connected and }|E(G)|=|V(G)|-1;\quad \forall i\ne j\in V(T),\ \exists!\text{ an }i\text{--}j\text{ path};\quad T+e\text{ contains exactly one cycle}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle bases, cocycle bases, and fundamental circuits and cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions relative to a maximal subgraph containing no undirected circuit; the introductory dimension claim is not asserted because it is not established within this extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family of undirected circuits is a cycle basis when its associated signed vectors form a basis of the cycle space; a family of undirected cuts is a cocycle basis when its associated signed vectors form a basis of the cocycle space. Let $G$ be directed or undirected and let $T$ be a maximal subgraph containing no undirected circuit. For each $e\in E(G)\setminus E(T)$, the unique undirected circuit in $T+e$ is the fundamental circuit of $e$ with respect to $T$. For each $e\in E(T)$, a set $X\subseteq V(G)$ can be chosen with $\delta_G(X)\cap E(T)=\{e\}$; the cut $\delta_G(X)$ is the fundamental cut of $e$ with respect to $T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle or cocycle basis is a family whose signed circuit or cut vectors form a basis of the corresponding space. Relative to a maximal undirected-acyclic subgraph, each edge outside it creates a unique fundamental circuit, and each edge in it determines a fundamental cut.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a directed or undirected graph}
T\subseteq G\text{ is maximal subject to containing no undirected circuit}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e\in E(G)\setminus E(T)\Rightarrow T+e\text{ contains a unique fundamental circuit},\qquad e\in E(T)\Rightarrow \exists X\subseteq V(G):\delta_G(X)\cap E(T)=\{e\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Trees, forests, and spanning trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions and elementary structural properties of finite undirected trees and forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph. A forest is an acyclic undirected graph, and each connected component of a forest is a tree. For a finite undirected graph \(G=(N,E)\), any two of connectedness, acyclicity, and \(|E|=|N|-1\) imply the third. Every connected graph contains a spanning tree. If an edge \(e\notin T\) is added to a spanning tree \(T\), it creates a unique cycle \(C\); for every \(f\in C\), \(T+e-f\) is again a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph, while a forest is an acyclic undirected graph whose connected components are trees. In a finite graph, any two of connectedness, acyclicity, and having one fewer edge than vertices imply the third. Every connected graph has a spanning tree. Adding a non-tree edge to a spanning tree creates one cycle, and removing any edge of that cycle again yields a spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is a tree}\iff G\text{ is connected and acyclic};\quad |E|=|N|-1\text{ for every tree};\quad T+e-f\text{ is a spanning tree for }f\in C(T+e).

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard finite nonempty undirected-graph definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph with \(V\neq\varnothing\). A set \(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree of \(G\) if the spanning subgraph \((V,T)\) is connected and contains no cycle. Equivalently, \(T\) is a spanning tree if and only if \((V,T)\) is connected and \(|T|=|V|-1\), or if and only if it is acyclic and \(|T|=|V|-1\). Such a set exists exactly when \(G\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite nonempty graph, a spanning tree is an acyclic connected subgraph containing every vertex; the graph has one exactly when it is connected.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(V\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree exactly when \((V,T)\) is connected and acyclic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shallow-light tree terminology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Context-dependent terminology for the trees satisfying the immediately preceding distance-stretch and total-weight guarantees, together with the source's qualitative tightness boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a connected undirected graph with $c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$, let $s\in V(G)$, and let $\epsilon>0$. A spanning tree $S$ satisfying $\operatorname{dist}_{(S,c)}(s,v)\le(1+\epsilon)\operatorname{dist}_{(G,c)}(s,v)$ for every $v\in V(G)$ and $\sum_{e\in E(S)}c(e)\le\left(1+\frac{2}{\epsilon}\right)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MST}}(G,c)$ is called a shallow-light tree. The source additionally states that this distance-cost tradeoff cannot be improved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree satisfying the preceding simultaneous source-distance and total-weight guarantees is called a shallow-light tree. The source states qualitatively that the tradeoff cannot be improved.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
S\text{ is a spanning tree satisfying the stated distance and cost bounds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is called a shallow-light tree; the stated distance-cost tradeoff cannot be improved.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(\delta(\mathcal P)\) denotes the edges with endpoints in different classes of \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph and \(k\in\mathbb Z_+\). The graph \(G\) contains \(k\) pairwise edge-disjoint spanning trees if and only if, for every partition \(\mathcal P\) of \(V\) into nonempty classes,
\[
|\delta(\mathcal P)|\ge k(|\mathcal P|-1).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An undirected graph contains k edge-disjoint spanning trees exactly when every partition of its vertices into nonempty classes has at least k times one less than the number of classes crossing edges.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal P\text{ ranges over partitions of }V\text{ into nonempty classes}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ contains }k\text{ edge-disjoint spanning trees}\iff \forall\mathcal P,\ |\delta(\mathcal P)|\ge k(|\mathcal P|-1)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Characterizations of spanning sets, bases, and hyperplanes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: All minimality and maximality assertions are with respect to set inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M be a matroid and X\subseteq E(M). Then: (i) X is spanning if and only if r(X)=r(M); (ii) X is a basis if and only if X is both spanning and independent; (iii) X is a basis if and only if X is an inclusion-minimal spanning set; and (iv) X is a hyperplane if and only if X is an inclusion-maximal non-spanning set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a matroid, spanning is equivalent to full rank; bases are exactly independent spanning sets and exactly minimal spanning sets; hyperplanes are exactly maximal non-spanning sets.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\iff V(T)=V(G);\qquad |E(T)|=n-1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycles, trees, subnetworks, and spanning trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for spanning structures, using the source's previously defined orientation-ignoring notion of path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cycle is a path \((n_1,\ldots,n_k)\) for which \(n_k=n_1\). A network is acyclic if it contains no cycle, and it is a tree if it is connected and acyclic. A network \((\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\) is a subnetwork of \((\mathcal N,\mathcal A)\) when \(\widetilde{\mathcal N}\subseteq\mathcal N\) and \(\widetilde{\mathcal A}\subseteq\mathcal A\). The subnetwork is a spanning tree when it is a tree and \(\widetilde{\mathcal N}=\mathcal N\). Relative to the fixed underlying network, a spanning tree can therefore be identified by its arc set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cycle is a path returning to its first node. An acyclic network contains no cycle, and a tree is connected and acyclic. A subnetwork uses subsets of the original nodes and arcs. It is a spanning tree when it is a tree containing every original node, so within a fixed network its arc set identifies it.
assumptions_latex: (\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\text{ is a candidate subnetwork of }(\mathcal N,\mathcal A).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\text{ is a spanning tree}\iff \widetilde{\mathcal N}=\mathcal N\text{ and }(\widetilde{\mathcal N},\widetilde{\mathcal A})\text{ is connected and acyclic.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Priority-queue implementation of Prim's algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implementation using vertex keys and INSERT, DECREASEKEY, and DELETEMIN operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a root \(v\), set \(T=(\{v\},\varnothing)\), and initialize \(l_w=\infty\) for \(w\ne v\). Whenever a vertex \(v\) enters \(T\), update each outside neighbor \(w\) so that \(l_w\) is the least weight of a currently known edge joining \(w\) to \(V(T)\), using \(\operatorname{INSERT}\) or \(\operatorname{DECREASEKEY}\). Repeatedly obtain a vertex of minimum key by \(\operatorname{DELETEMIN}\) and add an incident crossing edge of weight \(l_v\), until all vertices belong to \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain for each outside vertex the lightest known edge connecting it to the current tree. Use insert and decrease-key to maintain these values, repeatedly delete the minimum-key vertex, and add a crossing edge attaining its key until the tree spans the graph.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V(T)=V(G)\text{ after repeated minimum-key extensions of }T

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simultaneous exchange between two edge-disjoint spanning trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A rooted multi-edge exchange preserving both members of an edge-disjoint spanning-tree pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let T_1=(V,E_1) and T_2=(V,E_2) be edge-disjoint spanning trees and let r\in V. knowledge_statements.title: Spanning Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes nonmaximal spanning forests; maximality is characterized separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A set \(F\subseteq E\) is a spanning forest of \(G\) if the spanning subgraph \((V,F)\) is acyclic; isolated vertices are retained. It is a maximal spanning forest if no edge of \(E\setminus F\) can be added without creating a cycle. Equivalently, a spanning forest is maximal if and only if it restricts to a spanning tree on every connected component of \(G\), or, equivalently, if and only if \(|F|=|V|-c(G)\), where \(c(G)\) is the number of connected components of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning forest is an acyclic edge set on all vertices. Such a forest is maximal precisely when it spans each connected component by a tree, equivalently when it has |V|-c(G) edges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \((V,F)\) is acyclic, then \(F\) is maximal acyclic exactly when \(|F|=|V|-c(G)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Saturation Lemma for a Maximum Union of Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A maximality certificate for an unused edge in a maximum union of edge-disjoint forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $k\ge 1$, let $G$ be an undirected graph, and let $F=(F_1,\ldots,F_k)$ be a $k$-tuple of pairwise edge-disjoint forests maximizing $|E(F)|$, where $E(F)=\bigcup_{i=1}^kE(F_i)$. knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cycle-contraction algorithm for a maximum-weight rooted out-arborescence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the prescribed-root algorithm and separately records its failure to optimize directed forests without modification, plus the source's forest and unspecified-root variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(N,A)$ be an arc-weighted digraph with a prescribed root $r$ having no entering arc. Select, for every $v\neq r$, a maximum-weight arc entering $v$. If the selected arcs contain no cycle, they form an optimal spanning out-arborescence rooted at $r$. Otherwise, contract a selected directed cycle $C$ to a pseudonode $k$, discard self-loops, and replace every arc $(i,j)$ entering $C$ from outside by an arc $(i,k)$ of weight $w_{ik}=w_{ij}-(w_{i(j),j}-\delta)$, where $(i(j),j)$ is the selected arc of $C$ entering $j$ and $\delta=\min_{p\in C}w_{i(p),p}$. Repeat until the selected arcs are acyclic, and then expand pseudonodes in reverse contraction order, retaining all cycle arcs except the unique arc whose retention would give a vertex two entering arcs. The resulting structure is a maximum-weight spanning out-arborescence. This procedure need not produce a maximum-weight directed forest. For the forest variant, ignore arcs whose weights become negative under contraction; when a pseudonode with no selected entering arc is expanded, discard the lightest arc of its associated cycle. With no prescribed root, continue contracting until a pseudonode has no selected entering arc, then expand analogously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a heaviest incoming arc for each vertex other than the prescribed root. Contract any resulting directed cycle, adjust the weights of arcs entering it, and repeat. When the selected arcs become acyclic, expand the cycles in reverse order and omit the cycle arc that would duplicate an incoming arc. This returns a maximum-weight spanning tree directed away from the root. It does not necessarily maximize the weight of a directed forest; the forest variant ignores arcs made negative by contraction and drops the lightest cycle arc when expanding a pseudonode with no chosen incoming arc. The source also describes continued contraction for the case of an unspecified root.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is an arc-weighted directed graph}
r\in N\text{ is prescribed and has no entering arc in the rooted version}
\text{Every nonroot vertex of the spanning out-arborescence has exactly one selected entering arc}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The contraction--expansion procedure returns a maximum-weight spanning out-arborescence rooted at }r\text{; it requires the stated modifications for a forest or an unspecified root.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Acyclic digraphs, rooted directed trees, arborescences, and branchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directed trees and forests and their spanning arc-set forms; also records the source–sink property of nonempty finite acyclic digraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A digraph is acyclic if it has no directed circuit. Every nonempty finite acyclic digraph has at least one source and at least one sink. A directed tree is a digraph whose underlying undirected graph is a tree. It is rooted if it has precisely one source $r$; then every vertex $v\ne r$ has indegree $1$, and every vertex $v$ is joined to $r$ by a unique directed $r$-$v$ path. For $D=(V,A)$, an arborescence is a set $B\subseteq A$ such that $(V,B)$ is a rooted tree. A directed forest has an underlying undirected forest and is rooted if each weak component is a rooted tree. A branching is a set $B\subseteq A$ such that $(V,B)$ is a rooted forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An acyclic digraph has no directed circuit; if it is nonempty and finite, it has a source and a sink. A rooted directed tree has one source, and every other vertex has indegree one and a unique directed path from the root. An arborescence is a spanning rooted directed tree, while a branching is a spanning rooted directed forest.
assumptions_latex: B\subseteq A\text{ for the arborescence and branching definitions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ acyclic and }V\ne\varnothing\Rightarrow D\text{ has a source and a sink};\qquad B\text{ is an arborescence}\iff (V,B)\text{ is a rooted tree};\qquad B\text{ is a branching}\iff (V,B)\text{ is a rooted forest}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed 1-tree polytope and Held–Karp Lagrangian representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the directed 1-tree polytope and represents the optimum of the asymmetric subtour relaxation as a Lagrangian maximum over minimum directed 1-trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix vertex $1$ in a digraph $D=(V,A)$. The convex hull of directed 1-tree incidence vectors is described by $0\le x_a\le1$ for $a\in A$, $x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=1$ for every $v\in V$, $x(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(1))=1$, and $x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge1$ for every nonempty $U\subseteq V\setminus\{1\}$. Every Hamiltonian circuit is a directed 1-tree, and a minimum-length directed 1-tree is computable in strongly polynomial time. For $l\in\mathbb R^A$, define $l_y(u,v)=l(u,v)-y(u)$ and $f(y)=\min_F l_y(F)+y(V)$, where $F$ ranges over directed 1-trees. Then $\min\{l^Tx:x\text{ satisfies }(58.21)\}=\max_{y\in\mathbb R^V}f(y)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After fixing a root vertex, directed 1-trees have a cut-and-degree polyhedral description. Every directed Hamiltonian circuit is such a structure, and a minimum-cost directed 1-tree can be found in strongly polynomial time. Lagrangian multipliers on the nonroot outdegree conditions yield an exact max–min representation of the optimum of the asymmetric subtour relaxation.
assumptions_latex: D=(V,A)\text{ is a digraph with a fixed vertex }1
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\text{ is a directed 1-tree}\}=\{x:0\le x\le1,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v))=1,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{out}}(1))=1,\ x(\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(U))\ge1\},\quad \min_{x\text{ satisfying }(58.21)}l^Tx=\max_{y\in\mathbb R^V}f(y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reverse Search Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse traversal for target-directed reachability in a directed network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network \(G=(N,A)\) and target \(t\), initialize \(\mathrm{LIST}=\{t\}\). When examining a marked vertex \(j\), scan its incoming arcs and admit \((i,j)\) whenever \(i\) is unmarked and \(j\) is marked; mark and enqueue each such \(i\). The algorithm identifies exactly the vertices from which \(t\) is reachable by a directed path, and the selected discovery arcs form a directed in-tree rooted at \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting at a target vertex, repeatedly scan incoming arcs from unmarked tails into marked vertices. This finds exactly the vertices that can reach the target by directed paths, and the discovery arcs form a directed in-tree rooted at the target.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{i\in N:i\text{ is discovered}\}=\{i\in N:\exists\text{ a directed path from }i\text{ to }t\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reachability Lemma

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero-Cost Cycle-Contraction Arborescence Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-phase contraction-and-expansion algorithm for a prescribed-root minimum-cost arborescence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(v\neq r_0\), subtract from all arcs entering \(v\) their minimum entering-arc cost. Let \(S\) be the vertices reachable from \(r_0\) using only zero-cost arcs. If \(S\neq V\), find a directed zero-cost circuit \(C\subseteq V\setminus S\), contract \(C\), and repeat the cost-reduction step on the contracted digraph. Once every vertex is zero-reachable from \(r_0\), choose a spanning \(r_0\)-arborescence of zero-cost arcs in the contracted digraph and expand the contracted circuits in reverse order, obtaining a minimum-cost spanning \(r_0\)-arborescence of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize each nonroot vertex's incoming costs, repeatedly contract a zero-cost directed cycle outside the root's zero-reachable set, then build a zero-cost rooted arborescence in the contracted graph and expand the cycles in reverse order. The expansion yields a cheapest rooted arborescence.
assumptions_latex: r_0\in V\text{ is the prescribed root}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Reverse expansion of the zero-cost arborescence yields a minimum-cost spanning }r_0\text{-arborescence of }D.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Elementary Structural Properties of Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite graph and spanning-tree structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a subgraph of a graph having \(N\) nodes. (a) If \(T\) is acyclic and has at least one arc, then \(T\) has a leaf. (b) \(T\) is a spanning tree if and only if it is connected, has all \(N\) nodes, and has \(N-1\) arcs. (c) If \(T\) is a tree, every pair \(i,j\in V(T)\) is joined by a unique simple path. Adding an arc \(e\notin T\) whose endpoints lie in \(T\) creates a unique simple cycle, which may be oriented so that \(e\) is forward. (d) Deleting an arc \((i,j)\in T\) leaves two node- and arc-disjoint trees, one containing \(i\) and the other containing \(j\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite forest has a leaf; a connected subgraph on all N nodes is a spanning tree exactly when it has N−1 arcs; a tree has a unique simple path between every pair of nodes and adding one internal non-tree arc creates one simple cycle; deleting a tree arc separates the tree into two disjoint trees containing the respective endpoints.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a subgraph of a finite graph with }N\text{ nodes}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{gathered}(T\text{ acyclic},\ |A(T)|\ge1)\Rightarrow T\text{ has a leaf};\\ T\text{ spanning tree}\iff T\text{ connected},\ |V(T)|=N,\ |A(T)|=N-1;\\ T\text{ tree}\Rightarrow\text{unique paths, unique fundamental cycles, and two components after deletion of any tree arc.}\end{gathered}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted arborescences and rooted cuts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational definitions for an outward arborescence rooted at a fixed vertex and the associated cuts entering vertex sets not containing the root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph and let $r\in V$. A set $A'\subseteq A$ is an $r$-arborescence if its arcs form a spanning tree and every vertex in $V\setminus\{r\}$ is the head of exactly one arc in $A'$. Hence, for every $s\in V$, $A'$ contains a unique directed path from $r$ to $s$. A set $C\subseteq A$ is an $r$-cut if $C=\delta^-(V')$ for some nonempty set $V'\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}$. One $r$-cut may contain another, and inclusionwise minimal $r$-cuts may therefore be considered.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a digraph with fixed root r, an r-arborescence is a spanning tree in which every nonroot vertex is the head of exactly one selected arc. It has a unique directed path from r to every vertex. An r-cut is the set of arcs entering a nonempty vertex set that does not contain r. Rooted cuts may contain one another, so inclusionwise minimal rooted cuts are sometimes distinguished.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A'\text{ is an }r\text{-arborescence}\iff A'\text{ forms a spanning tree and every }v\in V\setminus\{r\}\text{ is the head of exactly one arc in }A';\qquad C\text{ is an }r\text{-cut}\iff \exists\,\varnothing\ne V'\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\text{ such that }C=\delta^-(V').

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Branchings and rooted out-arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions using the convention that arcs of a rooted arborescence point away from its root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A digraph \(G\) is a branching if its underlying undirected graph is a forest and \(|\delta^-(v)|\leq 1\) for every \(v\in V(G)\). A connected branching is an arborescence. If such an arborescence has \(n\geq1\) vertices, then it has \(n-1\) edges and exactly one vertex \(r\) satisfying \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\); this vertex is its root. If \((v,w)\) is an edge, then \(w\) is a child of \(v\), while \(v\) is the parent or predecessor of \(w\). A vertex without children is a leaf.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching has a forest as its underlying undirected graph and at most one entering arc at each vertex. A connected branching is an outward arborescence. Every nonempty such arborescence has n−1 arcs and a unique indegree-zero root. Arc heads are children of their tails, tails are their parents or predecessors, and vertices without children are leaves.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: G\text{ is a branching}\iff \underline{G}\text{ is a forest and }|\delta^-(v)|\leq1\ \forall v;\quad G\text{ connected branching}\Rightarrow |E(G)|=n-1\text{ and }G\text{ has a unique root.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability, spanning out-arborescence, and incremental-construction characterizations from a fixed root.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent characterizations of a rooted out-arborescence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural, rooted-reachability, minimality, cut, unique-walk, and indegree characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a digraph with \(|V(G)|=n\), and let \(r\in V(G)\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(G\) is an arborescence rooted at \(r\), meaning a connected branching with \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\); (b) \(G\) is a branching with \(n-1\) edges and \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\); (c) \(|E(G)|=n-1\) and every vertex is reachable from \(r\); (d) every vertex is reachable from \(r\), but deleting any edge destroys this property; (e) \(\delta^+(X)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(X\subsetneq V(G)\) with \(r\in X\), but deleting any edge destroys this property; (f) \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\) and there is a unique walk from \(r\) to every \(v\in V(G)\setminus\{r\}\); (g) \(\delta^-(r)=\varnothing\), \(|\delta^-(v)|=1\) for every \(v\neq r\), and \(G\) contains no circuit.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a digraph with root r, being an out-arborescence rooted at r is equivalent to being an n−1-edge branching with root indegree zero, having n−1 edges and reachability from r, being minimally root-reachable, satisfying the corresponding minimal outgoing-cut condition, having a unique walk from r to every other vertex, or satisfying the stated indegree and circuit conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (a)\iff(b)\iff(c)\iff(d)\iff(e)\iff(f)\iff(g).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rooted Cuts and Rooted Out-Arborescences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines rooted cuts and rooted spanning out-arborescences, states their inclusion-minimal cut-hitting characterization, and records the reachability condition for existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(D,\omega)$ be a weighted digraph and let $r\in V(D)$. For each nonempty $S\subseteq V(D)\setminus\{r\}$, the set $\delta^-(S)$ of arcs entering $S$ is an $r$-cut. An $r$-branching is a spanning arborescence oriented away from $r$. The inclusion-minimal arc sets meeting every $r$-cut are precisely the $r$-branchings. Moreover, an $r$-branching exists if and only if every vertex is reachable from $r$ by a directed path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a weighted digraph rooted at r, an r-cut is the set of arcs entering a nonempty vertex set not containing r. An r-branching is a spanning arborescence directed away from r. The inclusion-minimal arc sets meeting every r-cut are exactly the r-branchings, and such a branching exists exactly when every vertex is reachable from r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{X\subseteq A(D):X\text{ is inclusion-minimal and }X\cap\delta^-(S)\neq\varnothing\ \forall\,\varnothing\neq S\subseteq V(D)\setminus\{r\}\}=\{B:B\text{ is a spanning out-arborescence rooted at }r\},\quad (\exists B)\iff(\forall v\in V(D),\ r\leadsto v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Out-arborescence characterization and existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the convention that arcs are directed away from the root; the branching definition is included as a prerequisite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph. A branching is a set $B\subseteq A$ containing no undirected circuit and satisfying $|B\cap\delta^{\mathrm{in}}(v)|\leq 1$ for every $v\in V$. A branching is an arborescence when $(V,B)$ is weakly connected. Such a branching has a unique root $r$, and it is an $r$-arborescence equivalently when it is a directed spanning tree in which every vertex is reachable from $r$. Moreover, $D$ contains an $r$-arborescence if and only if every vertex of $D$ is reachable from $r$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching is an undirected-acyclic arc set with at most one selected arc entering each vertex. A weakly connected branching is an outward arborescence with a unique root. It is rooted at r exactly when every vertex is reachable from r in the selected directed spanning tree, and such a tree exists in the digraph exactly when every vertex is reachable from r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D\text{ contains an }r\text{-arborescence}\iff \forall v\in V,\;v\text{ is reachable from }r\text{ in }D.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc reversal exchanges the two rooted arborescence orientations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite digraph \(D=(V,A)\), define its reversal by \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}=(V,A^{\mathrm{rev}})\), where \(A^{\mathrm{rev}}=\{(v,u):(u,v)\in A\}\). For \(B\subseteq A\), let \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) contain the reversals of all arcs in \(B\). Then, for every root \(r\in V\), \(B\) is an out-arborescence of \(D\) rooted at \(r\) if and only if \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is an in-arborescence of \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}\) rooted at \(r\). Reversal is an involution and hence a bijection between these families.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing every arc bijectively converts rooted out-arborescences into rooted in-arborescences and preserves the root.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite digraph and \(r\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is an out-arborescence at }r\iff B^{\mathrm{rev}}\text{ is an in-arborescence at }r\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \text{For every digraph }D=(V,A),\text{ its branching polytope }P_B(D)\text{ has the integer decomposition property: for every }k\in\mathbb Z_+\text{ and }x\in kP_B(D)\cap\mathbb Z^A,\text{ there exist }x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(k)}\in P_B(D)\cap\mathbb Z^A\text{ such that }x=\sum_{i=1}^k x^{(i)}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every integer point in a positive-integer dilation of a digraph's branching polytope is a sum of that many integer points from the branching polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(k)}\in P_B(D)\cap\mathbb Z^A\text{ such that }x=\sum_{i=1}^k x^{(i)}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Criterion for Extending a Branching to a Rooted Spanning Arborescence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extendibility of a fixed branching within a rooted digraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $D=(V,A)$ be a digraph and let $r_0\in V$ have no entering arcs. A branching $(V,B)$ with $B\subseteq A$ extends to a spanning arborescence rooted at $r_0$ if and only if no set $Z\subseteq V\setminus\{r_0\}$ satisfies both $\varrho_B(Z)=0$ and $\varrho_B(v)>0$ for every arc $uv\in A$ entering $Z$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a digraph whose prescribed root has no entering arcs, a branching extends to a spanning arborescence rooted there exactly when there is no nonroot vertex set receiving no branching arc while the head of every available arc entering that set already has positive indegree in the branching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (V,B)\text{ extends to a spanning }r_0\text{-arborescence}\iff \nexists Z\subseteq V\setminus\{r_0\}:\ \varrho_B(Z)=0\ \land\ (\forall uv\in\delta_A^-(Z))\,\varrho_B(v)>0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Branchings and spanning root-set branchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines directed branchings, their root sets, and the spanning variant with a prescribed nonempty root set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A branching is a directed forest in which every vertex has in-degree at most one; its root-set is the set of vertices of in-degree zero. A branching with root-set R is the union of |R| vertex-disjoint arborescences. For a digraph D=(V,A) and \varnothing\neq R\subseteq V, a branching (V,B) in D is a spanning R-branching if its root-set is R. If R=\{r_0\}, it is a spanning arborescence rooted at r_0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A branching is a directed forest whose vertices have indegree at most one, and its roots are exactly the vertices of indegree zero. A spanning R-branching uses all vertices and has prescribed nonempty root set R; when R is a singleton, it is a spanning arborescence rooted at that vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (V,B)\text{ is a spanning }R\text{-branching iff it is a branching on }V\text{ with root-set }R.

knowledge_statements.title: Cobranchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-reversed counterpart of the chosen branching convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph. A cobranching is an arc set \(C\subseteq A\) such that the underlying undirected graph of \((V,C)\) is a forest and every vertex has outdegree at most one in \((V,C)\). Each nontrivial component is therefore an in-arborescence rooted at its unique vertex of outdegree zero; isolated vertices are roots of trivial components. Thus a cobranching is a vertex-disjoint spanning collection of inward-oriented rooted trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cobranching is an undirected forest whose arcs point toward one root in each component, so every vertex has outdegree at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\subseteq A\) is a cobranching exactly when its underlying graph is a forest and \(d_C^+(v)\leq 1\) for every \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: outdegree of v in the selected arc set C
cobranching arc set

children.title: Arc-Reversal Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Duality induced by reversing every arc in a directed forest.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Reversal Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc reversal exchanges branching and cobranching families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph and let \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}\) be obtained by reversing every arc. The map \(B\mapsto B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) preserves the underlying undirected forest and changes each indegree in \(B\) into the corresponding outdegree in \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\). Consequently, \(B\) is a branching of \(D\) if and only if \(B^{\mathrm{rev}}\) is a cobranching of \(D^{\mathrm{rev}}\). Since arc reversal is involutive, this correspondence is a bijection and preserves cardinality and component vertex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reversing all selected arcs bijectively maps branchings to cobranchings while preserving their undirected forest, size, and components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is a branching of }D\iff B^{\mathrm{rev}}\text{ is a cobranching of }D^{\mathrm{rev}}\).

notation.meaning: arc-reversed digraph
arcwise reversal of B

knowledge_statements.title: Graphic-Matroid Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bases of the cycle matroid for possibly disconnected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the graphic matroid \(M(G)\) has ground set \(E\) and independent sets equal to the edge sets containing no cycle. Its bases are precisely the inclusion-maximal forests of \(G\). Every basis \(B\) restricts to a spanning tree of each connected component of \(G\), and every such componentwise spanning forest is a basis. Hence all bases have cardinality \(r(M(G))=|V|-c(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graphic-matroid bases are exactly maximal forests: they contain a spanning tree of every connected component and have size vertices minus components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is a basis of }M(G)\iff B\text{ is a maximal forest of }G\).

notation.meaning: graphic or cycle matroid of G
number of connected components of G

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Independence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphic-matroid independence represented by acyclic edge sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(M(G)\) be its graphic matroid. For every \(I\subseteq E\), the set \(I\) is independent in \(M(G)\) if and only if the spanning subgraph \((V,I)\) is a forest. Consequently, the circuits of \(M(G)\) are exactly the edge sets of cycles of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge set is independent in the graphic matroid exactly when it is a forest; the matroid circuits are precisely the edge sets of graph cycles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\in\mathcal I(M(G))\iff (V,I)\text{ is a forest}\).

notation.meaning: graphic matroid of G

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generic Cut-Cycle Spanning-Tree Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An arbitrary-order hybrid of cut-based edge addition and circuit-based edge deletion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=\varnothing\) and \(G'=G\). Until \(F\) is a spanning tree, apply the following operations in any valid order: (A) choose a cut \(B\) of \(G\) with \(B\cap F=\varnothing\), choose a minimum-cost edge \(e\in B\), and add \(e\) to \(F\); (B) if \(G'\) contains a circuit \(C\), choose a maximum-cost edge \(e\in C\setminus F\) and delete \(e\) from \(G'\). Stop when \(F\) is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with an empty forest and the full current graph. In any valid order, either add a cheapest edge from a cut disjoint from the forest or delete a most expensive nonforest edge from a circuit of the current graph. Stop when the forest is a spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The procedure stops when }F\text{ is a spanning tree.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy forest-growth spanning-tree algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Kruskal-style rule of repeatedly adding a cheapest edge between distinct components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=(V,\varnothing)\). While \(F\) has more than one connected component, choose a minimum-cost edge whose endpoints lie in distinct components of \(F\), breaking ties arbitrarily, and add it to \(F\). Terminate when \(F\) is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with the edgeless forest and repeatedly add a cheapest edge joining two different current components, with arbitrary tie-breaking, until a spanning tree is obtained.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a connected edge-weighted graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_{k+1}=F_k+e_k,\quad e_k\in\arg\min\{c(e):e\text{ joins distinct components of }F_k\},\quad F\text{ terminates as a spanning tree}.

knowledge_statements.title: Basis–Tree Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connected-graph specialization of graphic-matroid bases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected graph and let \(M(G)\) be its graphic matroid. An edge set \(T\subseteq E\) is a basis of \(M(G)\) if and only if \((V,T)\) is a spanning tree of \(G\). Thus the identity map on edge subsets gives a bijection between the bases of \(M(G)\) and the spanning trees of \(G\). In particular, every basis and every spanning tree has cardinality \(|V|-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a connected graph, graphic-matroid bases and spanning trees are the same edge sets, each containing one fewer edge than vertices.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\text{ is a basis of }M(G)\iff T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\).

notation.meaning: graphic matroid of G
edge set under the basis–tree identification

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fundamental Cuts Relative to a Spanning Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cuts and spanning-tree exchanges induced by deleting tree edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G=(V,E)$ be connected with $|V|=n$, and let $T$ be a spanning tree of $G$. For each tree edge $f\in E(T)$, deleting $f$ separates $T$ into two subtrees with vertex sets $V_1$ and $V_2$. The set $\delta(V_1)=\{uv\in E:u\in V_1,\ v\in V_2\}$ is the fundamental cut associated with $f$ relative to $T$. There are $n-1$ such fundamental cuts. For every $e\in\delta(V_1)$, $(T-f)+e$ is a spanning tree of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a tree edge separates a spanning tree into two subtrees. The graph edges joining the two parts form the corresponding fundamental cut. There are n minus one such cuts, and adding any edge of the cut reconnects the parts into a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T-f\text{ has components with vertex sets }V_1,V_2;\qquad \delta(V_1)\text{ is the fundamental cut associated with }f;\qquad \#\{\text{fundamental cuts relative to }T\}=n-1;\qquad \forall e\in\delta(V_1),\ (T-f)+e\text{ is a spanning tree of }G.

knowledge_statements.title: Arborescences as Common Matroid Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-root out-arborescences as common bases on the arc set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a finite digraph with root \(r\), and suppose loops are excluded. Let \(M_g\) be the graphic matroid on \(A\) obtained by forgetting arc orientations, retaining parallel edges. Let \(M_r\) be the partition matroid whose independent sets contain no arc entering \(r\) and at most one arc entering each \(v\in V\setminus\{r\}\). After deleting arcs entering \(r\), both matroids have rank \(|V|-1\) whenever an out-arborescence rooted at \(r\) exists. Then \(B\subseteq A\) is such an out-arborescence if and only if \(B\) is a common basis of \(M_g\) and \(M_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-root out-arborescence is exactly a common basis of an underlying graphic matroid and a partition matroid enforcing one entering arc per nonroot vertex.
assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite loopless digraph with root \(r\in V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B\text{ is an out-arborescence rooted at }r\iff B\text{ is a common basis of }M_g\text{ and }M_r\).

notation.meaning: graphic matroid obtained by forgetting arc orientations
rooted entering-arc partition matroid
prescribed root

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contraction of a subset in a matroid
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines contraction using a basis of the contracted subset and records its graphic-matroid interpretation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let M=(S,\mathcal I), let B\subseteq S, and choose a basis J of B. Define S'=S\setminus B and \mathcal I'=\{J'\subseteq S':J'\cup J\in\mathcal I\}. The resulting system is the contraction construction; for a forest matroid, contracting an edge in the graph yields this construction on the contracted graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: To contract a subset B of a matroid, choose a basis J of B and declare a subset outside B independent exactly when adjoining J makes it independent in the original matroid. For forest matroids this agrees with graph edge contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S'=S\setminus B,\qquad \mathcal I'=\{J'\subseteq S':J'\cup J\in\mathcal I\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scan-first search and scan-first forest decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search procedure for directed reachability components and its undirected residual-forest iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In each stage on a digraph, choose an arbitrary root $s$, initialize it as reached, and repeatedly scan any reached but unscanned vertex $u$, adding every arc $uv$ whose head $v$ is not yet reached; the added arcs form a maximal arborescence spanning the vertices reachable from $s$. Repeat on the subdigraph induced by the remaining vertices. On an undirected graph $G$, one run produces a maximal forest $F_1$; repeating on $G-F_1,G-(F_1\cup F_2),\ldots$ produces a scan-first forest decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scan-first search scans any reached but unscanned vertex and adds edges to all newly reached heads, stage by stage producing maximal arborescences. On an undirected graph, repeated runs on residual edges produce a decomposition into maximal forests.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a finite digraph; for the forest specialization, }G\text{ is undirected}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Each directed stage yields a maximal arborescence, and repeated undirected runs yield a maximal forest decomposition }(F_1,F_2,\ldots).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Paired-Edge Forest Min–Max Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graphic specialization of matroid matching for forests constrained to be unions of prescribed edge pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(\mathcal P\) partition \(E\) into pairs. The maximum size of a forest \(F\subseteq E\) that is a union of classes of \(\mathcal P\) equals
\[

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Greedy Minimum-Weight Basis Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General matroid greedy algorithm, with Kruskal's algorithm as the graphic-matroid case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(E,\mathcal I)$ be a finite matroid with $E=\{e_1,\ldots,e_K\}$ ordered so that $w(e_1)\le\cdots\le w(e_K)$. Initialize $L=\varnothing$ and, for $j=1,\ldots,K$, replace $L$ by $L\cup\{e_j\}$ exactly when this union belongs to $\mathcal I$. The final set $L$ is a minimum-weight basis. For a graphic matroid, the independence test is that adding the edge creates no cycle, yielding Kruskal's algorithm.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Supermodularity of Minimum-Spanning-Tree Cost Under Edge Addition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Supermodularity of optimal spanning-tree cost as a function of the available optional edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $G$ have nonnegative edge costs $c$, let $T\subseteq V(G)$, and let $(T,U)$ be another graph with edge costs $c':U\to\mathbb{R}_+$. For $X\subseteq U$, let $m(X)$ be the cost of a minimum spanning tree in
\[
(T,E(G[T])\cup X),
\]
using $c$ on $E(G[T])$ and $c'$ on $X$. Assuming these minimum-spanning-tree costs are finite, $m:2^U\to\mathbb{R}_+$ is supermodular; that is, for all $A,B\subseteq U$,
\[
m(A)+m(B)\le m(A\cup B)+m(A\cap B).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When optional edges are added to a base graph on T, the minimum-spanning-tree cost, viewed as a function of the available optional-edge set, is supermodular.
assumptions_latex: (T,E(G[T])\cup X)\text{ admits a spanning tree for every }X\subseteq U.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall A,B\subseteq U,\qquad m(A)+m(B)\le m(A\cup B)+m(A\cap B).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Integral Partition-Packing Min–Max Formula for Minimum Spanning Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral min–max characterization of minimum spanning-tree length using partitions of the vertex set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sollin's Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization, componentwise minimum outgoing-edge selection, conditional merging, and termination rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $N_i=\{i\}$ for every $i\in N$ and $T^*=\varnothing$. While $|T^*|<n-1$, select for every current tree $N_k$ a minimum-cost outgoing arc $(i_k,j_k)$. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start with one tree per vertex. In each round, choose a cheapest outgoing edge for every current tree, then add a chosen edge and merge its endpoint trees only if they are still distinct. Stop when n minus one edges have been selected.

The optimal set \[F_w=\{x\in P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G):w^\top x=\tau\}\] is an exposed face of the spanning-tree polytope, and \[F_w=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\in\mathcal T(G),\ w^\top\chi^T=\tau\}.\] Its vertices are precisely the incidence vectors of minimum spanning trees. Consequently, the optimum is unique exactly when \(F_w\) is a singleton vertex; otherwise the optimal face has positive dimension.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning-tree solutions and network-simplex pivots
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the tree-basis representation, existence of an optimal tree solution, and the exchange operation underlying network simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a feasible minimum-cost-flow problem on a connected network with balanced node supplies and arc capacities. A spanning-tree solution is obtained by selecting a spanning tree \(T\), fixing every arc \(e\notin T\) at either \(x_e=0\) or \(x_e=u_e\), and solving the flow-balance equations for the arcs in \(T\). Whenever these equations are consistent, the tree-arc flows are uniquely determined. At least one optimal solution has this form. The network simplex method moves between spanning-tree solutions by introducing one nontree arc into the tree and removing one tree arc; these solutions and exchanges correspond, respectively, to linear-programming basic feasible solutions and simplex pivots.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible minimum-cost-flow problem on a connected network with balanced supplies, fix every non-tree arc at zero or at capacity. If the balance equations are consistent, they uniquely determine the flows on the spanning-tree arcs. An optimal spanning-tree solution exists, and network simplex moves between such solutions by exchanging one entering non-tree arc for one leaving tree arc. These solutions are linear-programming basic feasible solutions, and the exchanges are simplex pivots.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is connected and }T\subseteq E\text{ is a spanning tree}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Consistent balance equations uniquely determine }x_T;\ \exists\text{ an optimal spanning-tree solution, and network-simplex pivots exchange one entering nontree arc with one leaving tree arc.}

children.top_down_role: Tree substitutions organized through cycles created by entering edges.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected graph with weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(T\) is a minimum spanning tree, \(e\in E\setminus T\), and \(f\in P_T(e)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The exchange \(T-f+e\) is a spanning tree with weight \(w(T)+w(e)-w(f)\), and it is minimum if and only if \(w(e)=w(f)\).

notation.meaning: The unique tree path joining the endpoints of e.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(T'=T-f+e\) is a spanning tree and satisfies \(w(T')=w(T)+w(e)-w(f)\). Since \(T\) is minimum, \(w(f)\leq w(e)\) for every \(f\in P_T(e)\). Consequently, \(T'\) is also a minimum spanning tree exactly when \(w(f)=w(e)\); a strict inequality \(w(f)<w(e)\) makes the exchanged tree strictly heavier.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(T_1T_2\) to be an edge of \(\mathcal{X}(G,w)\) precisely when \(|T_1\triangle T_2|=2\). Then for any two minimum spanning trees \(T\) and \(T'\), there is a sequence \(T=T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_k=T'\) of minimum spanning trees such that \(|T_{i-1}\triangle T_i|=2\) for every \(i\). Thus all optimal trees lie in one component under weight-preserving fundamental-cycle exchanges.

children.title: Minimum Spanning Tree Verification
children.top_down_role: Recognition and certification of a proposed optimum.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite, connected, undirected graph with weights \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(T\subseteq E\) is a proposed spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(w(e)\geq\max\{w(f):f\in P_T(e)\}\) for all \(e\in E\setminus T\) certify that \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree.

notation.meaning: The unique path in T between the endpoints of e.
The proposed certificate tree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition of an MST by spanning-tree feasibility and fundamental-cycle inequalities.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Verify first that \(T\) is connected and has \(|V|-1\) edges. For every \(e\in E\setminus T\), compute the maximum edge weight on \(P_T(e)\). Accept \(T\) as minimum exactly when \(w(e)\geq\max\{w(f):f\in P_T(e)\}\) for every non-tree edge \(e\). The tree and these path-maximum comparisons form a finite certificate; any violated inequality identifies an improving exchange \(T-f+e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Verify tree feasibility and compare every non-tree edge with the heaviest edge on its tree path; all comparisons passing certifies optimality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent optimality certificates for a minimum spanning tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent path, fundamental-cut, and admissible edge-order characterizations of minimum-spanning-tree optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((G,c)\) be an instance of the minimum spanning tree problem, let \(T\) be a spanning tree of \(G\), and let \(n=|V(G)|\). The following are equivalent: (a) \(T\) is optimal; (b) for every \(e=\{x,y\}\in E(G)\setminus E(T)\), every edge \(a\) on the \(x\)-\(y\) path in \(T\) satisfies \(c(a)\leq c(e)\); (c) for every \(e\in E(T)\), if \(C\) is a connected component of \(T-e\), then \(e\) is a minimum-cost edge of \(\delta(V(C))\); (d) the edges can be ordered as \(E(T)=\{e_1,\ldots,e_{n-1}\}\) so that for every \(i\) there is an \(X\subseteq V(G)\) for which \(e_i\) is a minimum-cost edge of \(\delta(X)\) and \(e_j\notin\delta(X)\) for all \(j<i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree is minimum-weight exactly when it satisfies the path condition for every non-tree edge, equivalently the fundamental-cut condition for every tree edge, equivalently the stated cut-compatible ordering condition.
assumptions_latex: (G,c)\text{ is an instance of the minimum spanning tree problem}
T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathrm{(a)}\iff\mathrm{(b)}\iff\mathrm{(c)}\iff\mathrm{(d)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Array-based Prim algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct implementation on a complete weighted undirected graph using a closest selected neighbor for each unselected vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(U=\{v_1\}\), \(T=\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname{closest}[v]=v_1\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{v_1\}\). While \(U\ne V\), choose \(x\in V\setminus U\) minimizing \(d(x,\operatorname{closest}[x])\), set \(U\leftarrow U\cup\{x\}\) and \(T\leftarrow T\cup\{[x,\operatorname{closest}[x]]\}\), and replace \(\operatorname{closest}[v]\) by \(x\) whenever \(d(v,x)<d(v,\operatorname{closest}[v])\). Return \((V,T)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from one vertex, repeatedly attach the unselected vertex with the cheapest edge to the selected set, and update each remaining vertex's closest selected neighbor.
assumptions_latex: An undirected edge weight \(d_{ij}\) is given for every pair of vertices
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is the edge set returned when \(U=V\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path-optimality tree-exchange improvement algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes finite termination and the absence of a polynomial input-size running-time bound for this exchange procedure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) be a connected undirected graph with edge costs c and let T be any spanning tree. While there exist a non-tree edge (k,l) and an edge (i,j) on the unique k-l path in T such that c_{ij}>c_{kl}, replace (i,j) by (k,l). Each exchange strictly decreases the tree cost, so the procedure terminates after finitely many iterations at a minimum spanning tree. Its running time cannot in general be bounded polynomially in the size of the problem data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from any spanning tree, repeatedly insert a non-tree edge and remove a more expensive edge from its fundamental cycle. Every exchange lowers the cost, and finite termination yields a minimum spanning tree, but this procedure has no polynomial input-size running-time bound in general.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a connected undirected graph with edge costs }c
T\subseteq E\text{ is a spanning tree}
(k,l)\notin T,\ (i,j)\in P_T(k,l),\ c_{ij}>c_{kl}\text{ at each improving step}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\leftarrow T-(i,j)+(k,l)\text{ strictly decreases cost; repeated exchanges terminate finitely at an MST, without a polynomial input-size running-time bound in general.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Prim Algorithm for a Maximum-Weight Spanning Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded algorithm statement; the displayed initialization and updates require pairwise weights to be available, or an equivalent convention for absent edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(N,A)\) be a connected weighted undirected graph with root vertex \(1\). Assume the quantities \(w_{kj}\) used by the algorithm are defined, with absent edges represented by \(-\infty\) if necessary. Initialize \(P=\{1\}\), \(T=N\setminus\{1\}\), \(S=\varnothing\), \(u_j=w_{1j}\), and \(i(j)=1\) for \(j\in T\). Repeatedly choose \(k\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{j\in T}u_j\), move \(k\) from \(T\) to \(P\), add \((i(k),k)\) to \(S\), and, for every \(j\in T\) with \(w_{kj}>u_j\), set \(u_j=w_{kj}\) and \(i(j)=k\). When \(T=\varnothing\), \(S\) is a maximum-weight spanning tree of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Starting from vertex 1, repeatedly connect the remaining vertex having the heaviest currently available edge to the growing tree, then update the best connecting edges. For a connected weighted undirected graph, with absent edges handled consistently, the selected edges form a maximum-weight spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: G=(N,A)\text{ is a connected weighted undirected graph.}
w_{kj}\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{-\infty\}\text{ is defined whenever the algorithm compares }w_{kj},\text{ with }w_{kj}=-\infty\text{ permitted for absent edges.}
\text{Ties in the maximization may be resolved arbitrarily.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is a maximum-weight spanning tree of }G.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs a spanning tree by repeatedly selecting a cheapest edge leaving the current vertex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a connected undirected graph \(G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal E)\), \(|\mathcal N|=n\), and edge costs \(c_e\), choose one vertex and set \(\mathcal N_1\) equal to that singleton and \(\mathcal E_1=\varnothing\). For \(k<n\), choose
\[
e^*=\{i,j\}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}\{c_{\{u,v\}}:u\in\mathcal N_k,\ v\notin\mathcal N_k,\ \{u,v\}\in\mathcal E\},
\]
and set \(\mathcal N_{k+1}=\mathcal N_k\cup\{j\}\) and \(\mathcal E_{k+1}=\mathcal E_k\cup\{e^*\}\). Then every \((\mathcal N_k,\mathcal E_k)\) is a tree, and \((\mathcal N_n,\mathcal E_n)\) is a spanning tree.

c_e\text{ is specified for every }e\in\mathcal E

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MST Extendibility Invariant for Greedy Tree Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States that every intermediate tree produced by the greedy tree-growing algorithm can be extended to an MST.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense-Graph Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Array-based Jarník–Prim implementation for a connected dense undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\), edge weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and root \(r\), initialize \(S=\{r\}\), \(d(r)=0\), and \(d(v)=w(rv)\) when \(rv\in E\), otherwise \(d(v)=+\infty\). Repeatedly scan every vertex in \(V\setminus S\), choose one minimizing \(d(v)\), add its recorded predecessor edge to \(T\), insert \(v\) into \(S\), and update \(d(u)=\min\{d(u),w(uv)\}\) for all \(u\notin S\). When \(S=V\), output \(T\). The output is a minimum spanning tree, using \(O(n^2)\) weight comparisons and \(O(n)\) auxiliary storage when adjacency-matrix access is constant-time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Array-based Prim repeatedly scans all unchosen vertices for the cheapest crossing edge, producing a minimum spanning tree in quadratic time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned edge set \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree and is computed in \(O(n^2)\) time.

knowledge_statements.title: Priority-Queue Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heap-based Jarník–Prim implementation emphasizing sparse-graph complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) and root \(r\), assign keys \(d(r)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for \(v\ne r\), and place all vertices in a min-priority queue. Repeatedly extract a vertex \(v\) of minimum key, append its predecessor edge when \(v\ne r\), and for each unextracted neighbor \(u\) with \(w(uv)<d(u)\), set \(d(u)=w(uv)\), record predecessor \(v\), and perform decrease-key. The resulting edges form a minimum spanning tree. With adjacency lists and a binary heap the running time is \(O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)\), customarily \(O(|E|\log |V|)\) for connected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Heap-based Prim maintains the cheapest attachment key per unchosen vertex and constructs a minimum spanning tree efficiently on sparse graphs.
assumptions_latex: The queue supports extract-min and decrease-key.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a minimum spanning tree in \(O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)\) time with a binary heap.

notation.meaning: current attachment key of vertex v

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linked-list implementation of Kruskal component maintenance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component representation, weighted merging, and the resulting nonsorting running time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In Kruskal's algorithm, represent each current tree component by a singly linked list L with \operatorname{size}(L) and \operatorname{last}(L), and give each vertex i a pointer \operatorname{first}(i) identifying its component. Component equality tests over all m scanned edges take O(m) time. When joining components, append the smaller list to the larger and update \operatorname{first}(i) only for vertices of the smaller list. The total cost of all such updates is O(n\log n), so the implementation takes O(m+n\log n) time in addition to edge sorting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain every Kruskal component as a singly linked list with its size, last element, and a component identifier stored at each vertex. Test component equality in constant time and always append the smaller component to the larger. All scans cost O(m), all merges cost O(n log n), and the total time excluding sorting is O(m plus n log n).
assumptions_latex: \text{each merge appends the smaller component list to the larger one}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{membership}}=O(m),\quad T_{\mathrm{merges}}=O(n\log n),\quad T_{\mathrm{total}}=O(m+n\log n)+T_{\mathrm{sort}}.

knowledge_statements.title: Disjoint-Set Implementations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kruskal implementation using union–find for component maintenance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), make one disjoint-set singleton for each vertex, sort the edges into nondecreasing weight order, and initialize \(F=\varnothing\). For each edge \(uv\) in that order, test whether \(\operatorname{Find}(u)\ne\operatorname{Find}(v)\). If so, set \(F\leftarrow F\cup\{uv\}\) and apply \(\operatorname{Union}(u,v)\); otherwise discard the edge. The output is a minimum-weight spanning forest, and it is a minimum spanning tree when \(G\) is connected. Union by rank and path compression perform all disjoint-set operations in \(O((|V|+|E|)\alpha(|V|))\) time after sorting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kruskal uses union–find to accept an edge exactly when it joins different current components, yielding a minimum spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a minimum-weight spanning forest; if \(G\) is connected, \(F\) is a minimum spanning tree.

notation.meaning: accepted forest

children.title: Parallel Forest-Merging Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Parallel Forest-Merging Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weight-batched Kruskal variant permitting parallel processing without unsafe cyclic merges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition \(E\) into batches \(E_1,\ldots,E_k\) of equal weight, ordered by increasing weight. Before batch \(E_i\), contract every component of the forest \(F\) selected from earlier batches. In parallel, discard edges of \(E_i\) whose endpoints contract to the same vertex; on the resulting quotient multigraph choose any spanning forest \(H_i\), and lift its edges into \(F\). Then contract the new components and continue. Edges within \(H_i\) may be selected by any correct parallel spanning-forest routine. After all batches, \(F\) is a minimum-weight spanning forest of \(G\), and is a minimum spanning tree when \(G\) is connected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equal-weight edges are processed on the quotient of lighter-edge components; a parallel spanning forest of each batch safely merges components.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected weighted graph.
Each batch routine returns a spanning forest of its quotient graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accumulated set \(F\) is a minimum-weight spanning forest of \(G\).

notation.meaning: one equal-weight edge batch
forest selected in the batch quotient graph

knowledge_statements.title: Borůvka Component-Contraction Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical Borůvka phases with componentwise light-edge selection and contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(F=\varnothing\), with each vertex of a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) forming one component. In each phase, every current component \(C\) chooses a minimum-weight edge crossing \(\delta(C)\). Add a cycle-free maximal subset of the chosen edges to \(F\), merge their incident components, and equivalently contract the resulting components. Continue until one component remains. Every accepted edge is safe for some minimum spanning tree, so the final \(F\) is a minimum spanning tree. With consistent handling of duplicate choices, each nonterminal phase reduces the number of components by at least a factor of two, giving at most \(\lceil\log_2 |V|\rceil\) phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Borůvka repeatedly chooses a cheapest outgoing edge for every component and contracts the resulting forest, obtaining an MST in logarithmically many phases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns a minimum spanning tree after at most \(\lceil\log_2 |V|\rceil\) nonterminal phases.

children.title: Reverse-Delete Methods

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse-Delete Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descending-weight deletion algorithm for a connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), initialize \(H=G\) and order the edges by nonincreasing weight. Process each edge \(e\) once in that order. If \(H-e\) remains connected, replace \(H\) by \(H-e\); otherwise retain \(e\). After every edge has been considered, output \(E(H)\). The final graph is connected and contains no cycle, since the heaviest remaining edge of any cycle would have been deletable when processed. Consequently \(H\) is a spanning tree, and the cycle property implies that it has minimum total weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-delete examines edges from heaviest to lightest and removes an edge whenever connectivity survives; the remaining graph is an MST.
assumptions_latex: Edges are processed in nonincreasing weight order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The remaining graph \(H\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G\).

notation.meaning: current connected spanning subgraph
graph obtained by deleting edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reverse-delete algorithm fits the terminal container, but no inspectable citation is supplied. The statement also includes proof-style justification beginning with the cycle argument, contrary to the no-proof requirement.

children.title: Dual Greedy Viewpoint
children.top_down_role: Greedy interpretations based on removing edges rather than constructing a forest.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Greedy Viewpoint
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse-delete as greedy maximization in the cographic matroid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected and let \(M^*(G)\) be its cographic matroid. A set \(D\subseteq E\) is independent in \(M^*(G)\) exactly when \(G-D\) is connected. Thus reverse-delete, which scans edges by nonincreasing weight and inserts \(e\) into \(D\) whenever \(G-(D\cup\{e\})\) remains connected, is the ordinary maximum-weight greedy algorithm on \(M^*(G)\). At termination \(D\) is a maximum-weight cographic basis, while \(T=E\setminus D\) is a spanning tree. Since \(w(T)=w(E)-w(D)\), maximizing deleted weight is equivalent to minimizing retained tree weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-delete is maximum-weight matroid greedy on deletable edges; complementing the maximum-weight cographic basis gives a minimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D\) is a maximum-weight basis of \(M^*(G)\) if and only if \(E\setminus D\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G\).

notation.meaning: cographic matroid of G
deleted edge set
retained spanning tree

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cographic-matroid interpretation is mathematically appropriate for the dual greedy viewpoint, but the independence characterization and complementary-basis claim require an authoritative matroid source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reverse-Delete Algorithm for a Minimum Spanning Tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deletion-based greedy procedure for a connected edge-weighted undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting with a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), repeatedly select a maximum-cost edge that is not a cut-edge of the current graph and delete it. Each deletion preserves connectivity; continuing until no further deletion applies leaves a spanning tree.
