children.title: Deletion-Order Variants
children.top_down_role: Ordering regimes for cycle-preserving edge removal.

knowledge_statements.title: Deletion-Order Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order invariance subject to the nonincreasing-weight constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected, and let \(\preceq\) be any total edge order satisfying \(w(e)>w(f)\Rightarrow e\) is processed before \(f\). Starting from \(G\), process edges according to \(\preceq\) and delete an edge precisely when its deletion preserves connectivity. The retained edge set is a minimum spanning tree. Hence arbitrary permutation within each equal-weight class, as well as any implementation that realizes such a linear order, preserves optimality. If the processing order violates the nonincreasing-weight condition, the guarantee fails: on a weighted cycle, deleting a lighter edge before a heavier deletable edge can leave a nonminimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any reverse-delete order descending by weight is valid, including arbitrary tie orders; processing lighter edges too early can destroy optimality.
assumptions_latex: The order is nonincreasing in edge weight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every permitted deletion order returns a minimum spanning tree; unrestricted orders need not do so.

notation.meaning: total processing order on edges

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The order-invariance and failure-boundary claims fit the leaf and are stated consistently, but neither the reverse-delete result nor the counterexample claim has cited support.

children.title: Tied-Weight Deletion Regimes
children.top_down_role: Reverse-delete behavior when candidate edges have equal weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Tied-Weight Deletion Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correctness and possible nonuniqueness under tied edge weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the edges of a connected weighted graph into equal-weight classes and process the classes from greatest to least weight. Within a class, process edges in any order, deleting an edge exactly when the current graph remains connected. Every resulting retained set is a minimum spanning tree, although different within-class orders may produce different trees. All outputs have the same total weight. Distinct edge weights force a unique minimum spanning tree and therefore an order-independent output; with ties, uniqueness may still occur but is not guaranteed. Simultaneously deleting every individually deletable edge in a tied class is invalid unless their joint deletion is also verified to preserve connectivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tie order does not affect optimal weight but may change the returned MST; simultaneous deletions require a joint connectivity check.
assumptions_latex: Weight classes are processed from greatest to least.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sequential tie-breaking always yields an MST, whereas uncoordinated simultaneous deletion can disconnect the graph.

notation.meaning: edges having common weight lambda

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The tied-weight behavior and warning about simultaneous deletion fit the leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative citation or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Polytope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-set polytope of the graphic matroid for a finite simple graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(E(S)=\{uv\in E:u,v\in S\}\). The forest polytope is
\[P_{\mathrm{for}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F\in\{0,1\}^E:F\subseteq E\text{ is acyclic}\}.\]
It has the exact linear description
\[P_{\mathrm{for}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge 0}:x(E(S))\le |S|-1\text{ for every nonempty }S\subseteq V\right\}.\]
The singleton inequalities imply \(x_e\le 1\) by taking the two endpoints of \(e\). Every vertex of this polytope is therefore the incidence vector of a forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forest polytope is the convex hull of acyclic edge sets and is described exactly by nonnegativity and induced-subgraph rank inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite simple undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed rank-inequality system equals the convex hull of incidence vectors of forests in \(G\).

notation.meaning: edges induced by vertex set S
sum of x_e over edges e in A
incidence vector of edge set F

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and rank-inequality system fit the forest-polytope leaf, but the integrality claim lacks a source. The phrase “singleton inequalities” is inaccurate: the bound on an edge follows by taking the two-element set consisting of its endpoints.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard linear system describing the forest polytope is totally dual integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(x\ge0,\ x(E[U])\le |U|-1\ \forall\,\emptyset\ne U\subseteq V\bigr)\text{ is totally dual integral}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equates acyclic connectivity, unique paths, edge cardinality, and incremental leaf-edge construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a graph \(G=(V,E)\), the following are equivalent: (i) \(G\) is a tree; (ii) \(G\) is connected and contains no circuit; (iii) every pair of vertices is joined by a unique path; (iv) \(G\) is connected and \(|E|=|V|-1\); and (v) starting from any vertex, \(G\) can be constructed by successively adjoining edges such that exactly one endpoint of each newly adjoined edge belongs to the subgraph already constructed.

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds-style description of the spanning-tree polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a connected finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the spanning-tree polytope is
\[P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\subseteq E\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}.\]
It is exactly the face of the forest polytope having full graphic rank:
\[P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E_{\ge0}:x(E)=|V|-1,\;x(E(S))\le |S|-1\text{ for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\right\}.\]
Equivalently, using \(x(E)=|V|-1\), the rank inequalities may be expressed through appropriate partition or cut constraints. Its vertices are precisely the incidence vectors of spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spanning-tree polytope is the full-rank face of the forest polytope, defined by nonnegativity, total rank, and induced-subgraph inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, simple, undirected, and connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system is integral and equals \(P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)\).

notation.meaning: spanning-tree polytope of G
edges induced by S
incidence vector of tree T

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed spanning-tree polytope description is appropriate, but its exactness and integrality require a polyhedral source with a precise locator. The claimed equivalent partition or cut formulation is not actually stated.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spanning-Tree Polytope Description and Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete linear description of the spanning-tree polytope of a connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\) be a connected undirected graph and \(n=|V(G)|\). Then
\[
P=\left\{x\in[0,1]^{E(G)}:\sum_{e\in E(G)}x_e=n-1,\quad \sum_{e\in E(G[X])}x_e\le |X|-1\ \text{for every }\varnothing\ne X\subsetneq V(G)\right\}
\]
is integral, and its vertices are exactly the incidence vectors of the spanning trees of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every connected undirected graph, the unit-cube vectors having total edge value n−1 and satisfying every proper nonempty induced-subgraph rank inequality form an integral polytope whose vertices are precisely the spanning-tree incidence vectors.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is integral and }\operatorname{vert}(P)=\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Connector Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-hull model for connected spanning edge sets, without minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a connected finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), call \(C\subseteq E\) a connector when the spanning subgraph \((V,C)\) is connected. The connector polytope is
\[P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^C\in\{0,1\}^E:(V,C)\text{ is connected}\}.\]
Every point \(x\in P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\) satisfies \(0\le x_e\le1\) for \(e\in E\) and \(x(\delta(S))\ge1\) for every \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\). Its incidence vectors are upward closed: if \(C\) is a connector and \(C\subseteq C'\subseteq E\), then \(C'\) is also a connector. Inclusion-minimal connectors are exactly spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The connector polytope is the convex hull of connected spanning subgraphs; its inclusion-minimal incidence vectors are spanning trees.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\) models all spanning connectors, and its inclusion-minimal generating sets are spanning trees.

notation.meaning: connector polytope of G
cut with exactly one endpoint in S
incidence vector of connector C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and minimal-connector characterization fit the connector-polytope leaf, but no authoritative source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Tree Faces of Connector Polytopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The spanning-tree polytope is the minimum-cardinality face of the connected spanning-subgraph polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph, and let \(P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^F:F\subseteq E,\ (V,F)\text{ is connected}\}\). Every connected spanning edge set has at least \(|V|-1\) edges. Consequently, the valid inequality \(x(E)\ge |V|-1\) exposes the face \[P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\cap\{x:x(E)=|V|-1\}=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}.\] Thus the minimum-cardinality connector face is precisely the spanning-tree polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among connected spanning subgraphs, exactly those having the minimum possible number of edges are spanning trees; their convex hull is an exposed face of the connector polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{con}}(G)\cap\{x:x(E)=|V|-1\}=P_{\mathrm{ST}}(G)\).

notation.meaning: Incidence vector of the edge set F.
Sum of x_e over edges e in A.

children.title: Nonminimal Connector Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Nonminimal Connector Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonminimal connected subgraphs matter when edge costs are not nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^E\). If \(c_e\ge0\) for every \(e\in E\), each connected spanning edge set \(F\) contains a spanning tree \(T\subseteq F\) satisfying \(c(T)\le c(F)\); hence an optimal connector can be chosen as a tree. This reduction fails with negative costs: on a triangle with \(c_e=-1\) for all three edges, the full three-edge connector has cost \(-3\), whereas every spanning tree has cost \(-2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative costs permit pruning an optimal connector to a tree. Negative costs can make a connected spanning subgraph with extra edges strictly better than every tree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonminimal connectors are dispensable for \(c\ge0\), but not for unrestricted \(c\in\mathbb{R}^E\).

notation.meaning: Total edge cost over F.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The nonnegative-cost pruning statement and negative-cost triangle counterexample correctly express the nonminimal-connector boundary, but the record has no cited source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(|V|\ge 2\) and a vector \(x\in\mathbb{Q}_{\ge0}^E\), assign capacity \(x_e\) to edge \(e\). Compute a nontrivial global minimum cut \(\delta(S)\), where \(\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\). If \(x(\delta(S))<1\), output the violated connector inequality \(x(\delta(S))\ge1\). Otherwise certify that every inequality \(x(\delta(U))\ge1\), for \(\varnothing\ne U\subsetneq V\), is satisfied. The oracle therefore requires one polynomial-time global minimum-cut computation.

children.title: Integral Spanning-Tree Optimization

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Spanning-Tree Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edmonds' finite undirected spanning-tree polytope formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^E:x(E)=|V|-1,\ x(E(S))\le |S|-1\text{ for every }\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\}.\] Then \(P\) is integral and equals the convex hull of incidence vectors of spanning trees of \(G\). Hence, for every \(c\in\mathbb{Q}^E\), minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) has an integral optimal solution, and any such solution is the incidence vector of a minimum-cost spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The subtour description of the spanning-tree polytope is integral, so linear optimization over it returns a minimum-cost spanning tree.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^T:T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G\}\), and \(\min_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x\) has a tree-incidence optimum.

notation.meaning: Edges having both endpoints in S.
Incidence vector of tree T.

children.title: Separation–Optimization Interface
children.top_down_role: Relationship between inequality separation and optimization access.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation–Optimization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation and strong linear optimization are polynomial-time oracle equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be a nonempty bounded rational polyhedron whose facet complexity and containing-radius data are polynomially bounded in the binary input description. A strong separation oracle for \(P\) yields, via the ellipsoid method, a polynomial-time algorithm that either optimizes \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(P\) for rational \(c\) or reports \(P=\varnothing\). Conversely, a strong optimization oracle for \(P\) yields a polynomial-time strong separation oracle. Running time is polynomial in \(d\), the encoding lengths, and the relevant oracle complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For suitably encoded rational polyhedra, exact separation and exact linear optimization can each be implemented in polynomial time using an oracle for the other.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is a rational polyhedron with polynomially controlled encoding data.
Oracle inputs and outputs use binary rational encoding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation over \(P\) and strong linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomial-time oracle equivalent.

notation.meaning: Rational polyhedron under consideration.
Rational linear objective vector.

children.title: Fractional Relaxation Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Behavior of spanning formulations when integral structure is not enforced.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Relaxation Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Connectivity cut inequalities alone do not describe the connector polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=K_3\) and set \(x_e=\tfrac12\) for each of its three edges. Then \(0\le x_e\le1\) and every nontrivial cut has two crossing edges, so \(x(\delta(S))=1\). Thus \(x\) satisfies all connectivity cut inequalities. Nevertheless, every connected spanning subgraph of \(K_3\) has at least two edges, whereas \(x(E)=\tfrac32\). Hence \(x\) is not in the convex hull of connected spanning-subgraph incidence vectors, demonstrating that the cut relaxation is fractional.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half an edge on every side of a triangle satisfies all connectivity cuts but lies outside the connector polytope because its total edge mass is below two.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in\{y\in[0,1]^E:y(\delta(S))\ge1\}\) but \(x\notin P_{\mathrm{con}}(K_3)\).

notation.meaning: Convex hull of connected spanning-subgraph incidence vectors.
Cut induced by S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The triangle vector is a valid explicit counterexample and the counterexample content kind fits the relaxation-boundary container, but no inspectable source locator is supplied for the claimed polyhedral boundary.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Safe-edge extension by a minimum-cost cut edge

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a partial edge set can be extended to an MST, then adjoining a cheapest edge of any cut disjoint from that set preserves extendibility to an MST.

D\text{ is a cut and }D\cap B=\varnothing

children.title: Comparison Decision-Tree Model Pair
children.top_down_role: Comparison-based and instance-optimal complexity viewpoints.

children.title: Comparison-Based Complexity
children.top_down_role: Minimum spanning-tree complexity measured through edge-weight comparisons.

knowledge_statements.title: Comparison-Based Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kruskal's algorithm supplies a standard deterministic comparison upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a connected undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) with \(n=|V|\), \(m=|E|\), and totally ordered edge weights, Kruskal's algorithm first sorts all edges by nondecreasing weight and then accepts an edge exactly when it joins two current components. It returns a minimum spanning tree using \(O(m\log m)\) weight comparisons. Component tests implemented by disjoint-set union require \(O(m\,\alpha(m,n))\) additional operations and do not increase the number of weight comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sorting the edges and scanning them with disjoint-set union computes an MST using at most order m log m weight comparisons.
assumptions_latex: Edge weights belong to a totally ordered set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deterministic comparison complexity of exact MST is at most \(O(m\log m)\).

notation.meaning: Inverse-Ackermann disjoint-set complexity factor.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Kruskal comparison upper bound is standard and the complexity-bound kind fits the container, but the record supplies no algorithm-analysis source with a specific locator.

children.title: Decision-Tree Complexity
children.top_down_role: Branching computation models for distinguishing spanning-tree outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Tree Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic comparison decision trees for exact MST output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\). A deterministic MST comparison decision tree is a rooted tree whose internal nodes query whether \(w_e<w_f\), \(w_e=w_f\), or \(w_e>w_f\) for two edges \(e,f\in E\), and whose outgoing arcs represent the possible answers. Every leaf is labeled by a spanning tree and must label an MST for every weight vector consistent with its root-to-leaf transcript. Its worst-case complexity is its maximum leaf depth; the decision-tree complexity \(D(G)\) is the minimum such depth over all correct trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MST decision-tree complexity is the smallest worst-case number of pairwise weight comparisons needed by a correct comparison tree for a fixed graph.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
Comparisons are ternary and algorithms are deterministic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D(G)=\min_{\mathcal{T}}\max_{\ell\in L(\mathcal{T})}\operatorname{depth}(\ell)\), where \(\mathcal{T}\) ranges over correct MST comparison trees.

notation.meaning: Worst-case deterministic MST decision-tree complexity of G.
Leaves of decision tree T.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally coherent for a deterministic ternary comparison tree and fits the decision-tree container. A targeted source is nevertheless required to validate that this tie convention and leaf-output model are the intended literature model.

children.title: Instance-Optimal Comparison Bounds
children.top_down_role: Input-sensitive limits within comparison-based spanning-tree computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Optimal Comparison Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-wise instance optimality is measured against the best correct comparison tree for that graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each connected graph \(G\), let \(D(G)\) be the minimum worst-case depth of any deterministic comparison decision tree that correctly outputs an MST of \(G\). A uniform comparison algorithm \(A\) is graph-wise instance-optimal if there is an absolute constant \(C\) such that, for every connected \(G\), its worst-case number of weight comparisons satisfies \(C_A(G)\le C(D(G)+|E(G)|)\). A bound called instance-optimal must state this benchmark, the uniformity convention, and whether the additive input-inspection term is charged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph-wise instance optimality compares one uniform MST algorithm with the best decision tree specialized to each graph, while explicitly accounting for input inspection.
assumptions_latex: The comparison model and tie convention are fixed.
\(A\) is correct for every weighted connected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Instance optimality requires \(C_A(G)=O(D(G)+|E(G)|)\) uniformly over connected graphs \(G\).

notation.meaning: Worst-case comparisons made by algorithm A on graph G.
Optimal specialized decision-tree depth for G.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed benchmark, uniformity convention, and additive input-inspection term are literature-sensitive and unsupported. The record also states a definition or condition rather than an established instance-optimal complexity bound, so its selected content kind does not fully match the terminal container. A targeted source is needed before choosing the precise formulation and kind.

children.title: Noncomparison Model Boundary
children.top_down_role: Complexity changes when operations beyond pure weight comparison are available.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncomparison Model Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison bounds do not automatically transfer to integer or word-RAM models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose edge weights are \(b\)-bit integers stored on a word RAM with word size at least \(b+\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\). Kruskal's reduction computes an MST in \(O(m\,\alpha(m,n)+\operatorname{ISort}(m,b))\) time, where \(\operatorname{ISort}(m,b)\) is the cost of sorting \(m\) such integers using permitted word operations. Because integer sorting may use arithmetic, addressing, and bit operations unavailable to a comparison tree, a lower bound proved solely for pairwise comparisons is not, without a separate reduction, a lower bound in this model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Word-RAM algorithms can exploit integer representations, so comparison-tree lower bounds cannot automatically be interpreted as time lower bounds for integer-weight MST.
assumptions_latex: The word RAM permits unit-cost operations on sufficiently large words.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Comparison lower bounds do not transfer to the word-RAM MST model without an additional model-preserving argument.

notation.meaning: Time for sorting m integers of b bits in the specified RAM model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The qualitative failure boundary is correct, but the quantitative reduction and word-size assumption depend on the exact unit-cost operation set. No source is supplied to fix that model or support the stated running time.

children.title: Deterministic Near-Linear MST Methods
children.top_down_role: Deterministic contraction, partitioning, and specialized-data-structure families.

knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Near-Linear MST Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Borůvka contraction gives a deterministic exact near-linear baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a connected undirected weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) with a fixed tie-breaking order. Initialize each vertex as a component and \(F=\varnothing\). In every phase, select a minimum-weight outgoing edge of each current component, add a cycle-free subset of the selected edges to \(F\), and contract the resulting components. Stop when one component remains and output \(F\). Each phase preserves extendibility to an MST and at least halves the component count; scanning all edges per phase gives deterministic time \(O(m\log n)\) and space \(O(m+n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly adding cheapest outgoing component edges and contracting them produces an exact MST in logarithmically many linear-work phases.
assumptions_latex: Weights have a total order after deterministic tie-breaking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The contraction algorithm returns an MST in \(O(m\log n)\) time and \(O(m+n)\) space.

notation.meaning: Selected forest maintained by the algorithm.
Numbers of edges and vertices.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the methods container, but an arbitrary cycle-free subset of selected Boruvka edges need not halve the component count; maximality or an equivalent selection rule is required. Because the algorithm and bound lack a source, the precise corrected version should be aligned with a targeted reference.

children.title: Randomized Sampling-Filtering Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Randomized contraction and filtering families for sparse-time performance.

children.title: Randomized Edge Sampling
children.top_down_role: Randomized subgraph selection used to expose useful spanning-tree structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Edge Sampling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The MST sampling lemma bounds edges surviving sample-based filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have a fixed strict edge order. Independently sample each edge with probability \(p\in(0,1]\), forming \(H\), and let \(F\) be a minimum spanning forest of \(H\). An edge \(e=uv\) is \(F\)-light if \(u,v\) lie in different components of \(F\), or if its weight is no larger than the heaviest edge on the unique \(u\)-to-\(v\) path in \(F\). The expected number of \(F\)-light edges of \(G\) is at most \(n/p\). In particular, sampling with \(p=1/2\) leaves at most \(2n\) edges in expectation for subsequent filtering.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sample forest classifies only order n over p edges as light in expectation, enabling a sparse residual MST problem after filtering.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph with \(n=|V|\).
Edges are sampled independently with probability \(p\in(0,1]\).
Edge weights use a fixed strict tie-breaking order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[|\{e\in E:e\text{ is }F\text{-light}\}|]\le n/p\).

notation.meaning: Random sampled subgraph.
Minimum spanning forest of H.
Edge not heavier than the maximum edge on its forest path, with disconnected endpoints also light.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement resembles the standard MST sampling lemma and its variables and random experiment are explicit, but the constant, disconnected-forest convention, and exact light-edge definition require a targeted source. Since the principal claim is an expected-size bound, theorem or complexity-bound may fit more exactly than generic property after source verification.

children.title: Randomized Edge Filtering
children.top_down_role: Probabilistic elimination of edges irrelevant to an optimum tree.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite undirected weighted graph.
\(S\subseteq E\) is formed by independently retaining each edge with probability \(p\in(0,1]\).
\(F\) is a minimum spanning forest of \((V,S,w)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The retained instance is \(G'=(V,F\cup L_F,w)\), where \(L_F\) is the set of \(F\)-light edges.

notation.meaning: Maximum edge weight on the unique forest path from u to v, or positive infinity if no path exists.
Set of edges whose weight does not exceed their forest-path bottleneck.
Sample minimum spanning forest.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Filtering stage of the randomized sampling-filtering MST paradigm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each edge \(e=uv\in E\), define \(b_F(u,v)=\max\{w(f):f\in P_F(u,v)\}\) when \(u\) and \(v\) lie in one component of \(F\), and define \(b_F(u,v)=+\infty\) otherwise. Declare \(e\) to be \(F\)-light when \(w(e)\le b_F(u,v)\), and \(F\)-heavy otherwise. The filtering operation deletes every \(F\)-heavy edge and returns \(G'=(V,F\cup L_F,w)\), where \(L_F=\{e=uv\in E:w(e)\le b_F(u,v)\}\). An exact MST routine is then applied to \(G'\); disconnected inputs are handled componentwise as minimum spanning forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample edges, compute their minimum spanning forest, discard edges heavier than the corresponding forest-path bottleneck, and solve the remaining sparse instance.
knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Edge Filtering

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic description fits the filtering leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no citation supports the sampling-filtering construction or its exact tie convention. An inspectable source for the randomized MST filtering algorithm is required.

children.title: Sampling–Filtering Interface
children.top_down_role: Interaction between sampled structure and subsequent edge elimination.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a finite undirected weighted graph.
An edge is \(F\)-heavy only under a strict bottleneck inequality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every minimum spanning forest of \(G\) is contained in \(F\cup L_F\), so filtering preserves an optimum.

notation.meaning: Unique path in F between u and v, when it exists.
Set of F-light edges.
Graph remaining after the filter.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic correctness interface between sampled forests and exact MST computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_F\) contain every edge \(e=uv\in E\) for which \(u,v\) are disconnected in \(F\), or \(w(e)\le\max\{w(f):f\in P_F(u,v)\}\). If \(e\notin F\cup L_F\), then \(P_F(u,v)\cup\{e\}\) is a cycle on which \(e\) is strictly heaviest; hence \(e\) belongs to no minimum spanning forest of \(G\). Consequently every minimum spanning forest of \(G\) is contained in \(G_F=(V,F\cup L_F)\), and a minimum spanning forest computed in \(G_F\) is also optimal in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strictly forest-heavy edges cannot occur in an optimum, so the sample forest plus all forest-light edges preserves every minimum spanning forest.
knowledge_statements.title: Sampling–Filtering Interface

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preservation interface is plausible under the stated strict-heavy convention, but the record has no source for the cycle-property consequence or the claim that every minimum spanning forest is preserved.

children.title: Sparse-Graph Performance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Performance behavior on graphs remaining sparse after randomized reduction.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) has \(n\) vertices and arbitrary fixed edge weights.
Each edge is sampled independently with probability \(p\in(0,1]\).
\(F\) is a minimum spanning forest of the sampled graph, with consistent deterministic tie-breaking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expected number of \(F\)-light original edges is at most \(n/p\), and is \(O(n)\) for constant \(p\).

notation.meaning: Number of vertices.
Independent edge-sampling probability.
Set of F-light edges in the original graph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected sparsification regime underlying randomized linear-work MST algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under independent \(p\)-sampling, let \(F\) be a minimum spanning forest of the sampled graph and classify every original edge by its bottleneck on \(F\). The sampling lemma gives \(\mathbb{E}[|L_F|]\le n/p\). Therefore, for any constant \(p>0\), the filtered graph \((V,F\cup L_F)\) has \(O(n)\) edges in expectation. If filtering and the recursive or base-case MST computation use work linear in their input sizes, this estimate yields expected linear work per filtering level, including when the original graph is already sparse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent constant-rate sampling leaves only linearly many forest-light edges in expectation, so filtering remains effective even on sparse inputs.
knowledge_statements.title: Sparse-Graph Performance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the performance-regime leaf, but the exact expectation bound, its constant, and its tie-breaking assumptions require a locator for the MST sampling lemma.

children.title: Parallel-Distributed MST Regime Pair
children.top_down_role: Computation and communication models for exact spanning-tree construction.

children.title: Parallel MST Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact minimum spanning-tree computation using coordinated parallel processors.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is represented in a shared-memory comparison model.
Work counts primitive operations and depth counts the longest dependency chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An MST algorithm lies in the work-efficient polylogarithmic-depth regime when \(W(n,m)=O(m\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\) and \(D(n,m)=\operatorname{polylog} n\).

notation.meaning: Total number of primitive operations.
Parallel depth or span.
Processor count.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared-memory work-depth classification, not a claim about one particular parallel MST algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n=|V|\) and \(m=|E|\), classify a shared-memory MST algorithm by the pair \((W(n,m),D(n,m))\). It is work efficient when \(W(n,m)=O(m\,\operatorname{polylog} n)\), and it has polylogarithmic depth when \(D(n,m)=\operatorname{polylog} n\). On \(P\) processors, the corresponding scheduling target is \(T_P(n,m)=O(W(n,m)/P+D(n,m))\). A stronger linear-work regime requires \(W(n,m)=O(m)\); deterministic, randomized, CRCW, CREW, and EREW variants must be reported separately because their attainable bounds differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel MST regimes are classified by total work, dependency depth, processor count, memory discipline, and whether randomization is allowed.
knowledge_statements.title: Parallel MST Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a reasonable model-dependent classification condition, but no authoritative source fixes the work-depth model, scheduling bound, or meaning of the stated efficiency regime.

children.title: Distributed MST Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact minimum spanning-tree computation across networked participants.

assumptions_latex: The communication network is a connected weighted graph \(G=(V,E,w)\).
Each vertex initially knows its incident edges and identifiers.
Computation proceeds in synchronous rounds with bounded-size messages per edge per round.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A distributed MST bound is specified by its round complexity \(R(n,D)\), message complexity \(M(n,m)\), and message size \(B\).

notation.meaning: Hop diameter of the communication graph.
Number of synchronous communication rounds.
Total number of messages sent.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Synchronous message-passing classification for MST on the communication graph itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the synchronous bounded-message model, a distributed MST algorithm terminates after \(R\) rounds when every vertex has learned which of its incident edges belong to one common minimum spanning tree. Its regime is the tuple \((R(n,D),M(n,m),B)\), where \(R\) is the worst-case round count, \(M\) is the total number of transmitted messages, and each message contains at most \(B\) bits. Bounds must state whether identifiers and weights fit in \(B=O(\log n)\) bits and whether success is deterministic or holds with a stated probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributed MST regimes report rounds, total messages, message size, initial knowledge, and deterministic or probabilistic success guarantees.
knowledge_statements.title: Distributed MST Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the distributed-regime leaf, but the synchronous model, output convention, message-size convention, and complexity tuple have no cited source.

children.title: Work–Depth Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between aggregate computation and parallel critical-path length.

assumptions_latex: An MST computation is expressed as a directed acyclic graph of primitive operations.
\(W\) is the number of operations and \(D\) its longest dependency chain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The execution time satisfies \(T_P\ge\max\{W/P,D\}\), while greedy scheduling gives \(T_P=O(W/P+D)\).

notation.meaning: Total work of the computation.
Dependency depth or span.
Running time on P processors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic scheduling tradeoff applied to a parallel MST computation DAG.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Any schedule of an MST computation with work \(W\) and depth \(D\) on \(P\) processors satisfies \(T_P\ge W/P\) and \(T_P\ge D\). Under a greedy scheduler with unit-time operations and negligible scheduling overhead, \(T_P=O(W/P+D)\). Thus reducing depth below \(W/P\) does not asymptotically improve time at processor count \(P\), while decreasing work can improve both processor efficiency \(W/(PT_P)\) and running time. Work and depth claims remain model-dependent when concurrent reads or writes have nonconstant simulation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parallel time is constrained by both work per processor and dependency depth; greedy scheduling matches their sum up to constants.
knowledge_statements.title: Work–Depth Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The work-depth inequalities are standard, but this nontrivial complexity bound needs a specific source for the computation-DAG and greedy-scheduling assumptions.

children.title: Communication-Cost Regimes
children.top_down_role: Message and bandwidth costs in distributed spanning-tree construction.

assumptions_latex: A distributed MST algorithm runs on \(G=(V,E,w)\).
Messages traverse only communication edges of \(G\).
The message-size and synchrony conventions are fixed before comparing algorithms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Communication cost is represented by \((R,M,B,V_c)\), separating rounds, messages, bits per message, and per-edge congestion.

notation.meaning: Total number of messages.
Maximum number of bits in one message.
Maximum cumulative messages carried by one communication edge.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric representation for comparing communication costs; no universal optimal bound is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent the communication regime of a distributed MST algorithm by \((R,M,B,V_c)\). Here \(R\) is the number of synchronous rounds, \(M=\sum_{e\in E}M_e\) is the total number of messages, \(B\) bounds the bits per message, and \(V_c=\max_{e\in E}M_e\) is edge congestion accumulated over the execution. The total transmitted-bit cost is at most \(BM\). Algorithms are comparable under this representation only when they use the same initial-knowledge, message-size, synchrony, identifier, and weight-encoding conventions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Communication regimes separate latency, message volume, bit volume, and congestion, and are comparable only under the same distributed model.
knowledge_statements.title: Communication-Cost Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the communication-cost leaf, but the cumulative per-edge quantity denoted by V_c is not sourced and may not match standard congestion terminology.

children.title: MST Postoptimality Analysis
children.top_down_role: Behavior of optimal spanning trees under perturbation, deletion, and near-optimal selection.

children.title: Spanning Tree Replacement System
children.top_down_role: Single-edge failure and replacement structure for spanning trees.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exchange characterization of a unique shortest spanning tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The condition ranges over every feasible exchange of one tree edge for one non-tree edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: T\text{ is the unique shortest spanning tree of }G\iff\forall e\in T\;\forall f\in E\setminus T,\quad T-e+f\text{ spanning}\Longrightarrow l(f)>l(e).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree is uniquely shortest if and only if every feasible one-edge replacement introduces an edge strictly longer than the removed edge.
assumptions_latex: T\text{ is a spanning tree of }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T\text{ is the unique shortest spanning tree}\iff\forall e\in T\;\forall f\in E\setminus T,\ (T-e+f\text{ is a spanning tree})\Rightarrow l(f)>l(e)

children.title: Replacement Edges
children.top_down_role: Candidate non-tree edges for restoring spanning connectivity after a tree-edge failure.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a connected finite undirected weighted graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A minimum-weight replacement edge is any edge in \(\arg\min\{w(e):e\in\delta_T(f)\}\).

notation.meaning: Cut induced by deleting f from T, excluding f itself.
Set of minimum-weight replacement edges for f.
Weight function on graph edges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replacement edges for deleting one edge of a fixed spanning tree.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Deleting \(f\) partitions \(T\) into vertex sets \(A_f\) and \(V\setminus A_f\). Define \(\delta_T(f)=\{e=uv\in E\setminus\{f\}:u\in A_f,\ v\notin A_f\}\). Each edge \(e\in\delta_T(f)\) is a replacement edge for \(f\), and \(T-f+e\) is a spanning tree. Define the minimum replacement set by \(R_T(f)=\arg\min\{w(e):e\in\delta_T(f)\}\). If \(\delta_T(f)=\varnothing\), then \(f\) has no replacement and \(G-f\) is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A replacement edge crosses the cut exposed by deleting a tree edge; a minimum replacement has least weight among all such crossing edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Replacement Edges

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Replacement Paths
children.top_down_role: Alternative connection routes induced by a failed tree edge.

assumptions_latex: \(f=xy\in T\), and \(e=uv\in E\setminus T\) crosses the cut induced by \(T-f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique \(x\)-to-\(y\) replacement path in \(T-f+e\) is \(P_{T-f}(x,u)\cup\{e\}\cup P_{T-f}(v,y)\), up to exchanging the endpoint orientations.

notation.meaning: Unique path between vertices a and b in the indicated component of T-f.
Replacement path associated with f and e.
Replacement tree formed by exchanging f for e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-detour meaning of replacement path, fixed by the spanning-tree parent context.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose the endpoint labels so that \(x,u\) lie in one component of \(T-f\) and \(v,y\) lie in the other. Define the replacement path associated with \(f\) and \(e\) by \(Q_f(e)=P_{T-f}(x,u)\cup\{e\}\cup P_{T-f}(v,y)\). This is the unique \(x\)-to-\(y\) path in the replacement tree \(T-f+e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A replacement edge and the surviving tree paths form the unique detour between the endpoints of the failed tree edge.
knowledge_statements.title: Replacement Paths

children.title: Single-Edge Failure Regime
children.top_down_role: Postoptimal spanning-tree behavior under deletion of one edge.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a connected finite undirected weighted graph.
\(T\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G\).
Exactly one edge \(f\in T\) fails, while all weights remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(e_f\in\arg\min\{w(e):e\in\delta_T(f)\}\), then \(T-f+e_f\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G-f\).

notation.meaning: Cut exposed by deleting f from T, excluding f itself.
A minimum-weight replacement edge for f.
Total weight of an edge set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One failed edge of a previously computed MST; non-tree-edge and simultaneous failures are excluded.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\delta_T(f)\ne\varnothing\), choose \(e_f\in\arg\min\{w(e):e\in\delta_T(f)\}\). Then \(T_f=T-f+e_f\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G-f\), and \(w(T_f)=w(T)-w(f)+w(e_f)\). If \(\delta_T(f)=\varnothing\), then \(G-f\) is disconnected and has no spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After one MST edge fails, replacing it by the lightest edge crossing its exposed cut yields an MST of the surviving graph; if no replacement exists, the surviving graph is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Edge Failure Regime

children.title: Replacement-Cost Profiles
children.top_down_role: Cost variation across possible tree-edge replacements.

assumptions_latex: Replacement cost is evaluated separately for each \(f\in T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The replacement-cost profile is \(\rho_T(f)=\min_{e\in\delta_T(f)}w(e)\), and the failure penalty is \(\Delta_T(f)=\rho_T(f)-w(f)\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Minimum replacement-edge weight for f.
Increase in optimum weight after f fails.
Cut induced by deleting f from T.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Per-edge sensitivity profile for failures of edges in one fixed MST.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(f\in T\), define \(\rho_T(f)=\min\{w(e):e\in\delta_T(f)\}\), using \(\rho_T(f)=+\infty\) when the replacement set is empty. The replacement-cost profile is the vector \((\rho_T(f))_{f\in T}\). The associated failure penalty is \(\Delta_T(f)=\rho_T(f)-w(f)\). Since \(T\) is minimum, \(\Delta_T(f)\ge0\); when finite, the optimum value after deleting \(f\) equals \(w(T)+\Delta_T(f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The profile records each tree edge's cheapest replacement weight and the resulting increase in optimum spanning-tree cost after that edge fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Replacement-Cost Profiles

children.title: Near-Optimal Spanning Tree Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Alternative spanning trees immediately beyond the optimum.

children.title: Second-Best Spanning Trees
children.top_down_role: Spanning trees occupying the first objective level strictly beyond the optimum.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E,w)\) is a connected finite undirected weighted graph.
\(T\) is a minimum spanning tree of \(G\).
A second-best spanning tree means a spanning tree of minimum weight strictly greater than \(w(T)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Its excess weight is \(\Delta_2=\min\{w(e)-w(f):e\in E\setminus T,\ f\in P_T(e),\ w(e)>w(f)\}\), when this set is nonempty.

notation.meaning: Unique path in T joining the endpoints of e.
Minimum positive excess over the weight of T.
Total weight of the fixed minimum spanning tree.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictly heavier second-best tree; equal-weight alternative MSTs belong to the tied regime.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(e\in E\setminus T\), let \(P_T(e)\) be the unique path in \(T\) joining the endpoints of \(e\). Define \(\Delta_2=\min\{w(e)-w(f):e\in E\setminus T,\ f\in P_T(e),\ w(e)>w(f)\}\). If this set is nonempty, every minimizing pair \((e,f)\) defines a second-best spanning tree \(T_2=T-f+e\) satisfying \(w(T_2)=w(T)+\Delta_2\). If the set is empty, no spanning tree has weight strictly greater than \(w(T)\). Exchanges with \(w(e)=w(f)\) produce tied minimum spanning trees and are excluded from this strict convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly second-best spanning tree is obtained by a minimum positive single-edge exchange from an MST; zero-excess exchanges represent tied MST alternatives.
knowledge_statements.title: Second-Best Spanning Trees

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Near-Optimal Spanning Trees
children.top_down_role: Spanning trees lying within a prescribed objective neighborhood of the optimum.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
\(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\), and \(T^*\) is a minimum-weight spanning tree of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is \(\Delta\)-near-optimal exactly when \(w(T)\le w(T^*)+\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Total edge weight of the spanning tree \(T\).
Allowed additive optimality gap.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the additive-gap convention; multiplicative near-optimality is not included.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{T}(G)\) denote the finite set of spanning trees of \(G\), and write \(w(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\). A tree \(T\in\mathcal{T}(G)\) is an additive \(\Delta\)-near-optimal spanning tree if
\[
w(T)\le \min_{S\in\mathcal{T}(G)}w(S)+\Delta=w(T^*)+\Delta.
\]
The family of such trees is \(\mathcal{T}_{\Delta}(G,w)=\{T\in\mathcal{T}(G):w(T)-w(T^*)\le\Delta\}\). In particular, \(\mathcal{T}_{0}(G,w)\) is precisely the set of minimum spanning trees, including all tied optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree is additively near-optimal when its total weight exceeds the minimum spanning-tree weight by at most a prescribed nonnegative gap.
knowledge_statements.title: Near-Optimal Spanning Trees

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Ranked Spanning-Tree Alternatives
children.top_down_role: Objective-ordered organization of alternative spanning trees.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
\(\prec\) is a fixed total order on \(\mathcal{T}(G)\) used to resolve equal-weight ties.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), the \(k\)-th ranked alternative is the unique tree \(T_k\) occupying position \(k\) under the weight-and-tie ordering.

notation.meaning: The finite set of spanning trees of \(G\).
The number of spanning trees.
The tree at rank \(k\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ranks individual trees and resolves equal weights by a fixed auxiliary total order on the spanning-tree family.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{T}(G)\) be the finite set of spanning trees of \(G\), and let \(N=|\mathcal{T}(G)|\). Enumerate \(\mathcal{T}(G)=\{T_1,\ldots,T_N\}\) so that, for every \(i,j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\) with \(i<j\), either \(w(T_i)<w(T_j)\), or \(w(T_i)=w(T_j)\) and \(T_i\prec T_j\). This enumeration is the ranked spanning-tree representation. For every \(k\in\{1,\ldots,N\}\), \(T_k\) is the \(k\)-th ranked spanning-tree alternative. For every \(T\in\mathcal{T}(G)\), its rank is
\[
\operatorname{rank}(T)=1+|\{S\in\mathcal{T}(G):w(S)<w(T)\}|+|\{S\in\mathcal{T}(G):w(S)=w(T),\ S\prec T\}|.
\]
Without \(\prec\), weights determine ranked levels rather than unique individual ranks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sort the finite set of spanning trees by total weight and use a fixed total order on that set to resolve ties; the tree in position k is the kth ranked alternative.
knowledge_statements.title: Ranked Spanning-Tree Alternatives

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Tied Alternative Regimes
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity among spanning trees at the same nonoptimal objective level.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(j\in\{1,ldots,q\}\), the regime is tied at level \(\lambda_j\) exactly when \(|\mathcal{L}_j|>1\), and there are multiple minimum spanning trees exactly when \(|\mathcal{L}_1|>1\).

notation.meaning: The finite set of spanning trees of \(G\).
Distinct spanning-tree weights in increasing order.
Trees sharing the weight \(\lambda_j\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes ties by weight levels, independently of any tie-breaking order.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{T}(G)\) be the finite set of spanning trees of \(G\), and let \(\lambda_1<\cdots<\lambda_q\) be the distinct values attained by \(w(T)=\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\) over \(T\in\mathcal{T}(G)\). For every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\), define the weight level
\[
\mathcal{L}_j=\{T\in\mathcal{T}(G):w(T)=\lambda_j\}.
\]
The level \(\mathcal{L}_j\) is a tied alternative regime when \(|\mathcal{L}_j|>1\). The optimal regime is tied precisely when \(|\mathcal{L}_1|>1\). Ranking by distinct objective values assigns level rank \(j\) to every tree in \(\mathcal{L}_j\); consequently, tied trees share a level rank even though an auxiliary total order may assign them different individual ranks.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition the finite set of spanning trees into levels of equal total weight. A level is tied when it contains at least two trees, and multiple minimum spanning trees occur exactly when the lowest-weight level is tied.
knowledge_statements.title: Tied Alternative Regimes

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Weight-Perturbation Stability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Persistence and change of optimality under edge-weight perturbations.

children.title: Edge-Weight Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Changes in optimal spanning trees under individual edge-weight perturbations.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph with edge-weight map \(w:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
\(T\) is a minimum spanning tree of \((G,w)\).
Exactly one edge weight is changed by an additive amount \(\delta\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For the specified changed edge, the displayed path or fundamental-cut inequality is necessary and sufficient for \(T\) to remain a minimum spanning tree after the perturbation.

notation.meaning: The unique path in \(T\) between the endpoints of the non-tree edge \(e\).
The fundamental cut created by deleting the tree edge \(f\) from \(T\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives exact one-edge sensitivity intervals for retaining a fixed minimum spanning tree.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a non-tree edge \(e\in E\setminus T\), replacing \(w(e)\) by \(w(e)+\delta\) while leaving all other edge weights unchanged preserves the optimality of \(T\) if and only if
\[
w(e)+\delta\ge \max_{f\in P_T(e)}w(f).
\]
For a tree edge \(f\in T\), replacing \(w(f)\) by \(w(f)+\delta\) while leaving all other edge weights unchanged preserves the optimality of \(T\) if and only if
\[
w(f)+\delta\le \min\{w(e):e\in E\setminus T,\ e\text{ crosses }D_T(f)\},
\]
where the minimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). Equality permits an alternative minimum spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed minimum spanning tree survives a change to one edge weight exactly while the changed non-tree edge stays above its maximum path threshold or the changed tree edge stays below its minimum fundamental-cut replacement threshold.
knowledge_statements.title: Edge-Weight Sensitivity

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Optimality Stability Regions
children.top_down_role: Weight ranges over which a selected spanning tree remains optimal.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is minimum under \(c\) exactly when \(c\in\mathcal{R}_T\), a closed polyhedral cone.

notation.meaning: The unique path in \(T\) joining the endpoints of \(e\).
The weight-space region where \(T\) is minimum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the full weight-space stability region of one fixed spanning tree.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The optimality stability region of \(T\) is
\[
\mathcal{R}_T=\left\{c\in\mathbb{R}^{E}:c_e\ge c_f\text{ for every }e\in E\setminus T\text{ and every }f\in P_T(e)\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(c\in\mathcal{R}_T\) if and only if no exchange \(T-f+e\), with \(f\in P_T(e)\), has smaller total weight than \(T\). Thus \(T\) is a minimum spanning tree precisely throughout \(\mathcal{R}_T\). The region is a closed polyhedral cone; its relative interior corresponds to strict exchange inequalities and hence to uniqueness of \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tree remains minimum on the polyhedral weight region where every non-tree edge is at least as heavy as every tree edge on its fundamental cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimality Stability Regions

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Optimal-Tree Transition Points
children.top_down_role: Perturbation thresholds at which the optimal spanning-tree family changes.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
Edge weights vary affinely as \(w_e(t)=a_e t+b_e\) for \(t\) in an interval \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\).
Distinct spanning trees have distinct affine total-weight functions on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(t_0\in\operatorname{int}(I)\), an optimal-tree transition occurs exactly at a lower-envelope intersection where distinct spanning trees tie for minimum weight and exchange optimality across \(t_0\).

notation.meaning: Affine total weight of tree \(T\).
The set of minimum spanning trees at parameter \(t\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses a one-parameter affine perturbation with distinct tree-weight functions and defines two-sided transitions only at interior points of the parameter interval.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each spanning tree \(T\in\mathcal{T}(G)\), define
\[
W_T(t)=\sum_{e\in T}(a_e t+b_e),
\qquad
\mathcal{M}(t)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{T\in\mathcal{T}(G)}W_T(t).
\]
For \(t_0\in\operatorname{int}(I)\), call \(t_0\) an optimal-tree transition point when the optimal-tree set is not constant on any neighborhood of \(t_0\). Under the distinct-function assumption, this holds exactly when there exist distinct spanning trees \(T,S\in\mathcal{T}(G)\) such that
\[
W_T(t_0)=W_S(t_0)=\min_{R\in\mathcal{T}(G)}W_R(t_0)
\]
and the sign of \(W_T(t)-W_S(t)\) changes at \(t_0\). Thus the transition points are precisely the interior breakpoints of the lower envelope at which optimal trees exchange optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an interior parameter value with affine edge weights, an optimal-tree transition occurs exactly where distinct minimum tree-weight lines cross on the lower envelope and exchange optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Tree Transition Points

source_witnesses.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

children.title: Degenerate Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Stability behavior near tied weights or multiple optimal trees.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stability boundary is degenerate exactly when at least three distinct spanning trees are simultaneously optimal there.

notation.meaning: The set of minimum spanning trees under \(c\).
The stability region of tree \(T\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines degeneracy by three-or-more simultaneous optima, excluding ordinary two-tree boundaries.

source_refs.locator: Section 6.1. Minimum Spanning Trees p. 134

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\mathcal{M}(c)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{T\in\mathcal{T}(G)}\sum_{e\in T}c_e.
\]
A weight vector \(c\) lies on a stability boundary when \(|\mathcal{M}(c)|\ge 2\), equivalently when \(c\in\mathcal{R}_T\cap\mathcal{R}_S\) for distinct spanning trees \(T\) and \(S\). Such a boundary point is degenerate when \(|\mathcal{M}(c)|\ge 3\). At a degenerate point, several optimality cones meet, so a perturbation can select among more than two optimal-tree regimes; a point with exactly two optimal trees is a nondegenerate boundary under this convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stability boundary is degenerate when three or more spanning trees tie for minimum weight, so several optimality regions meet at the same weight vector.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Stability Boundaries

children.title: Directed Spanning Structures
children.top_down_role: The transition from undirected trees to contraction-based arborescence optimization.

assumptions_latex: \(D=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with root \(r\in V\).
Every vertex is reachable from \(r\), and each arc has real cost \(c(a)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The contraction-and-expansion procedure returns a minimum-cost spanning arborescence rooted at \(r\).

notation.meaning: A selected minimum-cost incoming arc of \(v\).
A directed cycle among the selected incoming arcs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the contraction algorithm for minimum-cost root-out arborescences.

source_refs.locator: 3.2 Cheapest trees and arborescences p. 105
Chapter 6. Spanning Trees and Arborescences p. 133

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(v\ne r\), choose a minimum-cost arc \(p(v)\) entering \(v\). If the selected arcs contain no directed cycle, output them. Otherwise contract a selected directed cycle \(C\). For every arc \((u,v)\) entering \(C\), assign reduced cost
\[
c'((u,C))=c((u,v))-c(p(v)),
\]
retain the costs of arcs leaving \(C\), and recurse on the contracted graph. Expand the recursive arborescence: if its entering arc for \(C\) corresponds to \((u,v)\), include that arc and all selected arcs \(p(x)\) of \(C\) except \(p(v)\). The resulting arcs form a minimum-cost spanning arborescence rooted at \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose cheapest incoming arcs, contract every resulting directed cycle with adjusted entry costs, solve recursively, and expand the contractions to obtain a minimum rooted arborescence.
knowledge_statements.title: Directed Spanning Structures

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Edmonds' Branching Algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contraction-and-expansion algorithm for nonnegatively weighted digraphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given G and c:E(G)\to\mathbb R_+, at stage i choose a maximum-weight subgraph B_i\subseteq G_i with |\delta_{B_i}^-(v)|\le1 for all v. If B_i has no circuit, stop. Otherwise contract every circuit C of B_i, retaining parallel arcs and assigning an arc e' induced by e=(v,w) the weight c_{i+1}(e')=c_i(e) when e' does not enter a contracted circuit, and c_{i+1}(e')=c_i(e)-c_i(\alpha(e,C))+c_i(e_C) when e' enters C, where \alpha(e,C)\in\delta_C^-(w) and e_C is a cheapest edge of C. Repeat, then expand contractions in reverse: for each C, add E(C)\setminus\{\alpha(e,C)\} if the current solution enters C through e, and add E(C)\setminus\{e_C\} otherwise. Output the expanded branching B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly select a maximum-weight subgraph of indegree at most one. If it contains cycles, contract all of them and adjust the weights of entering arcs by the specified cycle-edge and cheapest-edge correction. Once an acyclic solution is reached, expand the contractions in reverse, omitting the cycle edge associated with an entering arc or otherwise the cheapest cycle edge. The expanded solution is the algorithm's maximum-weight branching output.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}\{c(E(F)):F\text{ is a branching of }G\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cheapest Rooted Arborescence and Its Basic Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the nonnegative-cost rooted arborescence problem and records its shortest-path and undirected-MST specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=(V,A)\) be a digraph in which every vertex is reachable from a designated root \(r_0\), and let \(c:A\to\mathbb{R}_+\). The cheapest spanning \(r_0\)-arborescence problem is to find a spanning \(r_0\)-arborescence \(T\) minimizing \(\sum_{a\in T}c(a)\). A cheapest \(r_0t\)-path is obtained by adding zero-cost arcs \(tv\) for all \(v\in V\) and taking the unique \(r_0t\)-path in a cheapest arborescence of the extended digraph. Replacing every undirected edge by two oppositely directed arcs reduces the cheapest spanning-tree problem to this arborescence problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a digraph reachable from a prescribed root and nonnegative arc costs, find a spanning rooted arborescence of minimum total cost. The model contains nonnegative shortest paths and undirected minimum spanning trees through the stated zero-arc and bidirected-edge constructions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min\left\{\sum_{a\in T}c(a):T\text{ is a spanning }r_0\text{-arborescence of }D\right\},\quad\text{with the stated shortest-path and MST reductions}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: 1-Tree Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower bound obtained by decomposing a tour at a distinguished vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(V,E) have edge costs (c_e:e\in E), and fix v_1\in V. Define A=\min\{c_e+c_f:e,f\in\delta(v_1),\ e\ne f\}, and let B be the cost of a minimum spanning tree of G\setminus v_1. Whenever these quantities are defined, every traveling-salesman tour in G has cost at least A+B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fix a vertex. The sum of the two cheapest distinct incident-edge costs at that vertex and the cost of a minimum spanning tree after deleting the vertex is a lower bound on every TSP tour.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{TSP}}(G,c)\ge A+B

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Shallow-light spanning-tree tradeoff
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and computation of a spanning tree simultaneously approximating all source distances and minimum-spanning-tree cost; existence of an MST implicitly presupposes connectedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a connected undirected graph with edge weights $c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$, let $s\in V(G)$, and let $\epsilon>0$. There exists a spanning tree $S$ of $G$ such that, for every $v\in V(G)$, $\operatorname{dist}_{(S,c)}(s,v)\le (1+\epsilon)\operatorname{dist}_{(G,c)}(s,v)$ and $\sum_{e\in E(S)}c(e)\le\left(1+\frac{2}{\epsilon}\right)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MST}}(G,c)$. Such a tree can be computed in $O(m+n\log n)$ time, where $n=|V(G)|$ and $m=|E(G)|$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every positive epsilon, a connected undirected graph with R-plus-valued edge weights has a spanning tree whose distance from the source to every vertex is at most 1+epsilon times the corresponding graph distance and whose total weight is at most 1+2/epsilon times the minimum-spanning-tree cost. Such a tree is computable in O(m+n log n) time.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a connected undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists S\text{ spanning tree of }G:\ (\forall v\in V(G))\ \operatorname{dist}_{(S,c)}(s,v)\le(1+\epsilon)\operatorname{dist}_{(G,c)}(s,v),\quad \sum_{e\in E(S)}c(e)\le\left(1+\frac{2}{\epsilon}\right)\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{MST}}(G,c),\quad S\text{ is computable in }O(m+n\log n).

children.title: Degree-Constrained Spanning Trees
children.top_down_role: Spanning-tree variants with vertex-degree restrictions.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
Each vertex has an integer degree bound \(b_v\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution minimizes total cost among spanning trees satisfying \(\deg_T(v)\le b_v\) for every \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: Degree of vertex \(v\) in tree \(T\).
Prescribed upper degree bound at \(v\).

review_flags: auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses vertex-specific upper bounds; uniform maximum-degree constraints are the special case \(b_v=B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The degree-constrained minimum spanning-tree problem is
\[
\min_{T\in\mathcal{T}(G)}\ \sum_{e\in T}c(e)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\deg_T(v)\le b_v\quad\text{for every }v\in V.
\]
A spanning tree satisfying all degree inequalities is feasible. If no such tree exists, the instance is infeasible. The uniform degree-bounded version takes \(b_v=B\) for all \(v\), while vertex-specific bounds permit heterogeneous restrictions. The constraints concern degrees in the selected tree, not degrees in the ambient graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-cost spanning tree whose degree at every vertex does not exceed its prescribed upper bound.
knowledge_statements.title: Degree-Constrained Spanning Trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The bounded-degree spanning-tree formulation is standard, precise, and correctly classified as a definition, but the record supplies no source reference. A dedicated source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator is required before candidate-review acceptance.

children.title: Diameter-Constrained Spanning Trees
children.top_down_role: Spanning-tree variants with limits on maximum tree distance.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution minimizes total cost among spanning trees with \(\operatorname{diam}(T)\le D\).

notation.meaning: Number of edges on the unique path between \(u\) and \(v\) in \(T\).
Maximum pairwise tree distance.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard unweighted-diameter constrained spanning-tree formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Measures diameter by hop count in the selected tree, not by edge costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a spanning tree \(T\), let \(d_T(u,v)\) be the number of edges on its unique \(u\)-to-\(v\) path and define
\[
\operatorname{diam}(T)=\max_{u,v\in V}d_T(u,v).
\]
The diameter-constrained minimum spanning-tree problem is
\[
\min_{T\in\mathcal{T}(G)}\ \sum_{e\in T}c(e)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
\operatorname{diam}(T)\le D.
\]
Thus feasibility requires every pair of vertices to be connected within at most \(D\) tree edges. If no spanning tree satisfies this bound, the instance is infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-cost spanning tree in which every pair of vertices is separated by at most D tree edges.
knowledge_statements.title: Diameter-Constrained Spanning Trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hop-count diameter formulation is mathematically precise and matches the terminal container, but the record has no source reference. The standard-field rationale cannot replace a cited source for this review layer.

children.title: Hop-Constrained Spanning Trees
children.top_down_role: Spanning-tree variants with limits on path edge counts.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
A root \(r\in V\) and integer hop bounds \(h_v\ge 0\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible solution minimizes total cost among spanning trees satisfying \(d_T(r,v)\le h_v\) for all \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: Number of edges on the unique root-to-\(v\) path in \(T\).
Maximum permitted root-to-\(v\) hop count.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard rooted hop-constrained spanning-tree formulation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses rooted, vertex-specific hop limits; a common limit is obtained by setting every \(h_v=H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The rooted hop-constrained minimum spanning-tree problem is
\[
\min_{T\in\mathcal{T}(G)}\ \sum_{e\in T}c(e)
\quad\text{subject to}\quad
d_T(r,v)\le h_v\quad\text{for every }v\in V,
\]
where \(d_T(r,v)\) counts the edges on the unique path from \(r\) to \(v\) in \(T\). A uniform hop limit \(H\) is obtained by taking \(h_v=H\) for every \(v\ne r\) and \(h_r=0\). Feasibility concerns distance from the designated root, unlike a diameter constraint, which bounds every vertex pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a minimum-cost spanning tree whose unique path from the designated root to each vertex respects that vertex's hop limit.
knowledge_statements.title: Hop-Constrained Spanning Trees

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The rooted, vertex-specific hop-constrained formulation is coherent and correctly distinguished from a pairwise diameter constraint, but no source is cited. A dedicated scholarly locator is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Paths, circuits, connectivity, and cut vertices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic path and vertex-connectivity terminology for undirected graphs, including simplification of paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A path in \(G\) is a sequence \(P=v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k\) such that the endpoints of \(e_i\) are \(v_{i-1}\) and \(v_i\) for every \(1\le i\le k\). It is closed if \(v_0=v_k\), edge-simple if \(e_1,\ldots,e_k\) are distinct, simple if \(v_0,\ldots,v_k\) are distinct, and a circuit if it is closed, \(k\ge1\), and \(v_0,\ldots,v_{k-1}\) are distinct. Its length is \(k\). Whenever a path joins \(u\) and \(v\), a simple path joins them. The graph \(G\) is connected if every pair of vertices is joined by a path. In a connected graph, \(v\) is a cut vertex if \(G\setminus v\) is disconnected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A path alternates vertices and incident edges; it may be closed, edge-simple, or vertex-simple. A circuit is a nonempty closed path with no repeated vertex before returning to its start, and path length is the number of edges. Any two vertices joined by a path are joined by a simple path. A graph is connected when every vertex pair is joined, and a cut vertex is one whose deletion disconnects a connected graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: u\text{ and }v\text{ joined by a path}\implies u\text{ and }v\text{ joined by a simple path};\quad G\text{ connected}\iff\forall u,v\in V(G)\ \exists\text{ a }(u,v)\text{-path}.

children.title: Combined-Constraint Regimes
children.top_down_role: Spanning-tree variants subject to multiple structural restrictions simultaneously.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite connected undirected graph with edge costs \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\).
Bounds \(b_v\), \(D\), and rooted hop bounds \(h_v\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A tree is feasible exactly when it simultaneously satisfies all degree, diameter, and rooted hop inequalities.

notation.meaning: The family of spanning trees satisfying every imposed constraint.
Tree distance measured in number of edges.
Designated root for hop constraints.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conjunction of standard side-constrained spanning-tree predicates
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines degree, hop-count diameter, and rooted hop constraints in one feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a root \(r\in V\). The combined feasible family is
\[
\mathcal{F}=\left\{T\in\mathcal{T}(G):
\deg_T(v)\le b_v\ \forall v\in V,
\ \max_{u,v\in V}d_T(u,v)\le D,
\ d_T(r,v)\le h_v\ \forall v\in V
\right\}.
\]
The combined-constraint problem minimizes \(\sum_{e\in T}c(e)\) over \(T\in\mathcal{F}\). A tree is feasible only when all displayed predicates hold simultaneously; satisfying any proper subset is insufficient. The instance is infeasible when \(\mathcal{F}=\varnothing\). Omitting a constraint family is modeled by assigning nonbinding bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A combined regime minimizes tree cost while enforcing degree limits, a pairwise diameter bound, and rooted hop limits simultaneously.
knowledge_statements.title: Combined-Constraint Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conjunction of degree, diameter, and rooted hop predicates is precise, and condition is an appropriate content kind for the combined-regime leaf. However, the record has no source reference, so the standard-field rationale is insufficient for acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Steiner Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Undirected, edge-weighted Steiner tree with a prescribed terminal set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be an undirected graph, let \(R\subseteq V\) be a nonempty terminal set, and let \(c:E\to\mathbb{R}\) be edge weights. A Steiner tree for \(R\) is a tree \(T=(V_T,E_T)\) with \(R\subseteq V_T\subseteq V\) and \(E_T\subseteq E\). Vertices in \(V_T\setminus R\) are Steiner vertices. A minimum-weight Steiner tree minimizes \[c(E_T)=\sum_{e\in E_T}c(e)\] over all such trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Steiner tree connects all prescribed terminals and may use additional graph vertices; its minimum-weight version minimizes the total weight of selected edges.
assumptions_latex: At least one connected subgraph of \(G\) contains \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is feasible exactly when it is a tree in \(G\) whose vertex set contains \(R\), and optimality minimizes \(\sum_{e\in E_T}c(e)\).

notation.meaning: prescribed terminal set
Steiner vertices used by the tree
total selected-edge weight

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Steiner-tree leaf, but no citation establishes the intended convention, particularly the use of arbitrary real rather than nonnegative edge weights.
